artworks.title: Pink Field & the Flute Player
artworks.description: Manjit Bawa's works are easily recognisable for their distinctly individualistic style. The artist started his career as a silk screen printer but experimented over the decades with his artistic style and techniques skirting with abstraction, Tantric art forms, usage of textured layers and contorted human limbs in his works to emerge as one of the nation's foremost figurative painters. Manjit Bawa finally arrived at his indisputable style of painting formable human forms, round and supple in their essence and exuding gentle warmth and compassion.

artworks.description: Om Prakash Sharma is known for his contribution to the contemporary art and especially to the tradition of Tantra in the modern art of India. His canvases are predominant with intense contrasting color applications with geometric shapes concentric towards the focused center on the canvas, carrying a strong symbolism in the forms created.

artworks.title: I Beyond
artworks.description: The Delhi based figurative painter and a noted muralist, in his paintings have a keen presence of man's socio-historical being. His human figures are expressively stylized, have a monumentality, even in the small painted formats. The pictorial space in his paintings bring out figures with his fine overlaps of colours in a range of tones. In this work 'I Beyond' has a similar effect in the figure emerging out of the solid bold background with the other figures intertwined with the main human self, seen in the overlaps of the colour applications.

metadata.inscription: Bireshwar Sen was a miniaturist and a landscape painter. His landscapes have the power to transmute the chaotic nature to a cosmos of enchanting forms of mountains, dense valleys, clouds, etc. The eternal himalayan range is a leitmotif in his works. This landscape also represents the mountain range in the blue grey dawn. All the landscapes of his gives the viewer to travel in the scenic compositions of nature.

artworks.title: Oh Lord Bless Our Son
artworks.description: Bireswar Sen's paintings are spiritual offerings to the grandeur of almighty nature. The collection of National Gallery of Modern Art, Delhi has a number of miniature landscapes by Bireswar Sen, mostly executed in watercolour and tempera on a card size paper not exceeding two and a half by three and a half inches. Bireswar Sen started his artistic career as a figure painter, following the beliefs of Bengal school. Soon abandoning religious and mythological subjects, he indulged in seeking harmony among the forces of nature in his works. As a result, the figures in his compositions also became smaller, making natural surroundings the focal points of the compositions.

artworks.title: Reality Or Unreality, 1977
artworks.description: Stephen Sacklarian was an Armenian American artist who practiced both painter and sculpture. His works are considered to be a blend of modern art styles of Abstract expressionism and Cubism. Earlier in his creative process his works were realistic but but he turned towards to abstraction soon. His paintings are typically filled with biomorphic forms in the foreground in front of angular room like backgrounds or dark colour fields. The forms residing in the room like spaces in his paintings are abstraction of human and animal forms, limbs, faces, etc. The subconscious mind is a dominant thread in Sacklarianâ??s works which looks dream like. The subconscious mind is a dominant thread in Sacklarianâ??s works which looks dream like.

artworks.title: Mountain And The Hermit
artworks.description: Nandalal's work reflects changing landscapes, portraits of people, sketches from life and places at the time of changing outlook in the modern Indian cultural domain. His nature to explore the various materials and mediums allowed him to make a prolific body of work in different mediums. Along with his explorations of art learning from the style of the Tagores, he also imbibed the techniques of art from the European indigenous tradition and the Japanese wash technique. He was inspired by the painting style of Abanindranath Tagore which can be seen in this work in the manner he deals with the landscape, the colour wash technique, and composition.

artworks.description: B.N. Arya was an exponent of the watercolour wash technique and the imagery of the Neo Bengal school. His paintings reflect his inspiration of the epic Puranic and the ancient kavya themes, along with the reflection of poor and common working people in his works. Going beyond the representational imagery in he works, he explores the semi abstract and abstract style of working, with which he explored the themes of life and shadows of death and decay.

artworks.title: Painting-A
artworks.description: Damodaran transforms nature into a joyous memory, creating a dream world like imagery. He was inspired by the landscape of his native land, Kerala. His works look abstract with a prominent use of colours and line, are biomorphic landscapes. Though when the element of line is considered, he negates the line and marks is only in the contours of the coloured forms intertwined or overlapping each other. This rendering brings a haziness in his landscapes and transforms the reality to dreamy imagery.

artworks.title: Untitled, 1982
artworks.description: Gulam Rasool Santosh is the most important artist from the movement known as neo-tantra in Indian art. After a few years of painting figurative and abstract works in the mould of the other Indian Progressives, Santosh’s art changed dramatically towards tantra when he had a mystical experience in the Amarnath cave in 1964. From then on, until his death in 1997, G. R. Santosh dedicated his life to the study and practice of tantra, a yogi as much as an artist.

artworks.title: Mother and Child - IV (A Tribute to Mother Teresa)
artworks.description: M.F Husain's paintings are characterised by bold lines, free use of colours and his experimentation with various materials and themes. The print shows a mother with her children, dressed in a blue bordered white saree, the signature of Mother Teresa, the missionary and social worker, a symbol of humility. The figures are delineated in modernist style with sharp, bold colour strokes defining the contours and suggesting her stance.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Husain' twice, in English and Hindi along the lower margin of the painting.

artworks.title: At rest
artworks.description: Ramkinkar Baij was a reclusive modernist artist who always remained on the fringes of the art market. He took a great interest in human figures, body language and in the general human drama. Modern Western art and pre and post-classical Indian art were his main points of reference. Although primarily known for his expressionistic sculpture, he was also a gifted painter. The sense of rhythm that his sculpture was noted for is manifested brilliantly in his paintings and sketches. His works in the Kalighat tradition interconnected with Cubism to achieve an unusual personal idiom. Both his sculpture and his paintings are unprompted and bold.

artworks.title: Sunset At Jhelum, 1958
artworks.description: The sun is setting, and its soft orange hue is reflected in the River Jhelum in Kashmir. Boatmen in their shikaras are coming ashore. The oil on canvas has the men in the foreground, and the river, bathed in muted shades of the dipping sun, in the background. The painting is a picture of calm. Nature was often Sailoz Mookherjea’s muse. The artist, who taught at the Sarada Ukil School of Art, New Delhi, and was later with the Art Department of Delhi Polytechnic, often discussed the spirit of nature with his students. Now well-known names, the students recall fondly how he introduced them to the concept of colour, and the nuances of nature.

artworks.title: Three Graces
artworks.description: Krishna Reddy's prints have an emphasis on line to express the physical form of his subjects infused with vibrant hues. In the above abstract print Reddy has depicted the Greek mythological characters of the three graces, goddesses of charm, beauty, and creativity. It is an alluring example of Reddy's mastery over the viscosity technique of printmaking. A process that uses the principle of viscosity to print multiple colours of ink from a single plate, rather than relying upon multiple plates for colour separation.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Krishna Reddy' along the lower margin of the print. There is also an inscription in English that reads, 'Three Graces' along the lower margin.

artworks.title: The Knock, 1969
artworks.description: Hore's work are filled by humanist eye, inclination towards empathy, and his communist ideology. Tension in lines and emaciating figures were significant in most of his works. He was driven with the feeling of anguished and suffering of the poor. The overall impression one gets from Somnath’s works is the depth of poverty he has starved in. He used knives and red-hot rods to cut and burn into a piece of clay, which then provided the basis for a cement mould that would shape and scar the paper pulp. He moulded the white paper to form wound-like gashes, and stained them with red blood-like pigment. The haunted imagery, blisters of the restrained figures made him poignant among others. Hore stated,' I do not make pictures, I make 'wounds' indeed.

Along with his explorations of art learning from the art of the Tagores and Ajanta murals, he also imbibed the techniques of art from the European indigenous tradition and the Japanese wash technique. artworks.title: Floating the Canoe, Gopalpur
artworks.description: This painting belongs to a series of monochromatic ink and watercolour paintings inspired by the Sumi-e Japanese technique the artist employed in the last phase of his life. These compositions were stripped to the bare minimum where only a few strokes of ink were employed to create natural forms in an effortless approach. In the above painting Nandalal has executed two fishermen floating the canoe. He has used similar brushwork in the rendering of the sea and the figures, thus conveying the idea of nature and humans as different expression of the same underlying unity. This painting was purchased from the collection of Shri Biswaroop Bose and Smt. Nivedita Bose, children of Nandalal Bose.

artworks.title: Dhaki, 1937
artworks.description: Dhaki belongs to the NGMA collection of Nandalal Bose’s landmark set of temperas popularly known as the Haripura Posters. Painted on Mahatma Gandhi’s invitation, these posters were meant for decorating the venue of the 1937 Congress session at Haripura, a village in Gujarat. Gandhi, a strong believer of the social relevance of art, wanted the posters to depict the lives of ordinary people who would be at the venue. Bose immersed himself in the everyday life of Haripura, recording all in quick sketches. These were the basis of 400 panels which were then painted by Bose and his students. Bose himself painted 80. Among the many artisans he brought to life, here is a drummer or a dhaki. The tempera is drawn in direct, bold lines and resembles the traditional ‘pata’ paintings of Bengal in its simplicity of form and flat colouring.

artworks.title: Prophet (PIR)

artworks.title: Fisher Men In The Sea, 1949
artworks.description: Nandalal's work reflected changing landscapes, portraits of people, sketches from life and places at the time of changing outlook in the modern Indian cultural domain. Along with the techniques of art he imbibed from the European indigenous tradition and the Japanese wash technique, he also explored the art of Rabindranath Tagore, Abnindranath, who was his teacher. Thus the techniques of their art also reflect in Nandalal's visual expressions. This work depicting the fishermen at the sea, reflect the oriental techniques as well as Abanindranath's style seen the colour washes and the brush work.

artworks.title: A PROCESSION
artworks.description: Nandalal preferred drawing from life, often sketching outdoors with the subject being life, nature studies, landscapes, figure drawings and animals. In the above print, the artist has depicted a procession in which men and women are walking carrying a canopy, sacred pots over the head, musical instruments and food. The composition is rendered with firm yet fluid lines gauged on the linoleum sheet and printed on a plain surface, creating a dramatic contrast of black and white image, resulting in an effective means of documenting the royal procession.

artworks.title: Waves, 1947
artworks.description: Nandalal's work depicts changing landscapes, portraits of people, sketches from life and places at the time of changing outlook in the modern Indian cultural domain. His nature to explore the various materials and mediums allowed him to make a prolific body of work in different mediums. He painted many indigenous landscapes with ink wash technique. Most of his landscapes also carry the sign with a seal by the artist like in the Chinese paintings made with wash techniques. The landscapes captured the atmosphere; its vastness, calmness, etc in the lines and tones he used in treating it. Every landscape painted by him, be it a black and white rendering, is unique and documented with great detail. Every landscape painted by him, be it a black and white rendering, is unique and documented with great detail.

artworks.title: MAHAPRASAD
artworks.description: The above monochrome watercolour illustration by Nandalal depicts two men serving Mahaprasad to a group of people sitting in a row on the floor. The composition is rendered with bold, fluid brush strokes to delineate the contours of the forms. The strokes are diluted further to achieve tonal variation from darker to grey, a technique Nandalal learned from the arts of the Far East .

artworks.title: GEESE
artworks.description: Nandalal had a firm belief that for the creation of art an intimate understanding of nature and its way is imperative. He made instantaneous visual records of anything amusing happening in his surroundings, the subjects being life, nature studies, landscapes, figure drawings, animals. In this drawing, Nandalal has depicted two geese in soft water colour patches to bring out the subject from the background without demarcating much details.

artworks.title: DURGA WITH HALLOW OF FIRE
artworks.description: In this representation of Durga mounted on her lion, Bose depicts her fierce avatar with multiple arms, each with a weapon. She is drawn against a reddish brown background with bold, linear ink strokes that articulate her extraordinary energy, strength and valour. She is the powerful demon-slayer who took on a mighty opponent and defeated him. According to historians, Durga became a cultural icon in Bengal during the nationalist movement which also saw a period of religious and social upheavals. A prayer to her was infused with social and cultural meanings as she became the mother goddess whose worship pierced through walls of class, gender and caste. As in many of his other works, Nandalal Bose’s portrayal of Durga is highly ornamental. The swirling lines, the portrayal of the lion and the symbols of fire are reminiscent of Bose’s fascination with oriental art.

artworks.title: Kenduli Fair, 1928
artworks.description: Nandalal's work depicts changing landscapes, portraits of people, sketches from life and places at the time of changing outlook in the modern Indian cultural domain. His nature to explore the various materials and mediums allowed him to make a prolific body of work in different mediums. He painted many indigenous landscapes with ink wash technique. Most of his landscapes also carry the sign with a seal by the artist like in the Chinese paintings made with wash techniques. The landscapes captured the atmosphere; its vastness, calmness, etc in the lines and tones he used in treating it. Every landscape painted by him, be it a black and white rendering, is unique and documented with great details like this work showing the sketch of the tree branch at the Kenduli fair.

These compositions were stripped to the bare minimum where only a few strokes of ink were employed to create natural forms in an effortless approach. Nandalal was keen to capture the rhythm and pattern in the varied images of nature. The above painting belongs to the 'Mountains' series and was purchased from the collection of Shri Biswaroop Bose and Smt. Nivedita Bose, children of Nandalal Bose.

metadata.inscription: Signed and dated '16.12.61 Nanda' in Bengali vertically in the top-right corner of the painting with brush in black colour. The painting also bears the artist's personal seal in red.

artworks.title: A Landscape
artworks.description: Nandalal's work depicts changing landscapes, portraits of people, sketches from life and places at the time of changing outlook in the modern Indian cultural domain. His nature to explore the various materials and mediums allowed him to make a prolific body of work in different mediums. He painted many indigenous landscapes with ink wash technique. Most of his landscapes also carry the sign with a seal by the artist like in the Chinese paintings made with wash techniques. The landscapes captured the atmosphere; its vastness, calmness, etc in the lines and tones he used in treating it. Every landscape painted by him, be it a black and white rendering, is unique and sketched with great detail. Every landscape painted by him, be it a black and white rendering, is unique and sketched with great detail.

His nature to explore the various materials and mediums allowed him to make a prolific body of work in different mediums. He painted many indigenous landscapes with ink wash technique. Most of his landscapes also carry the sign with a seal by the artist like in the Chinese paintings made with wash techniques. The landscapes captured the atmosphere; its vastness, calmness, etc in the lines and tones he used in treating it, be it a black and white rendering. This work, despite its simplistic delineation, is a very interesting and a playful depiction of man on the horse hunting the pig.

artworks.title: A Boat
artworks.description: This painting belongs to a series of monochromatic ink and watercolour paintings inspired by the Sumi-e Japanese technique the artist employed in the last phase of his life. These compositions were stripped to the bare minimum where only a few strokes of ink were employed to create natural forms in an effortless approach. Nandalal was keen to capture the rhythm and pattern in the varied images of nature. The above painting belongs to the 'Boat' series and was purchased from the collection of Shri Biswaroop Bose and Smt. Nivedita Bose, children of Nandalal Bose.

metadata.inscription: Signed and dated '12.11.59 Nanda' in Bengali vertically in the bottom-left corner of the painting with brush in black colour. The painting also bears the artist's personal seal in red.

artworks.title: Mountains
artworks.description: Nandalal's work depicts changing landscapes, portraits of people, sketches from life and places at the time of changing outlook in the modern Indian cultural domain. His nature to explore the various materials and mediums allowed him to make a prolific body of work in different mediums. He painted many indigenous landscapes with ink wash technique. Most of his landscapes also carry the sign with a seal by the artist like in the Chinese paintings made with wash techniques. The landscapes captured the atmosphere; its vastness, calmness, etc in the lines and tones he used in treating it. Every landscape painted by him, be it a black and white rendering, is unique and done with detailed observation.

artworks.title: A Boat
artworks.description: Nandalal's work depicts changing landscapes, portraits of people, sketches from life and places at the time of changing outlook in the modern Indian cultural domain. His nature to explore the various materials and mediums allowed him to make a prolific body of work in different mediums. He painted many indigenous landscapes with ink wash technique. Most of his landscapes also carry the sign with a seal by the artist like in the Chinese paintings made with wash techniques. Every landscape painted by him, be it a black and white rendering, is unique and a documented study.

artworks.description: Nandalal preferred drawing from life, often sketching outdoors with the subject being life, nature studies, landscapes, figure drawings, animals or anything that he found fascinating. The subject here being 'A Boat' executed from his memory and experiences. These compositions were stripped to the bare minimum where only a few strokes of ink were employed to create natural forms in an effortless approach. This painting was purchased from the collection of Shri Biswaroop Bose and Smt. Nivedita Bose, children of Nandalal Bose.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' and dated '7 Bu' (referring to the day of the week, Wednesday) in Bengali in the top-right corner of the painting with brush in black colour. The painting also bears the artist's personal seal in red.

artworks.title: A BOAT
artworks.description: This painting belongs to a series of monochromatic ink and watercolour paintings inspired by the Sumi-e Japanese technique the artist employed in the last phase of his life. The subject here being 'A Boat' executed from his memory and experiences. These compositions were stripped to the bare minimum where only a few strokes of ink were employed to create natural forms in an effortless approach. As K.G. Subramanyan writes of Nandalal's work in the book, 'Vision and Creation', "The art object is not a representation of the natural object, it is a variable equivalent. Its reality lies in its life rhythm and sense of complete authenticity, even when it lacks verisimilitude."

artworks.title: The Sun
artworks.description: Nandalal's work depicts changing landscapes, portraits of people, sketches from life and places at the time of changing outlook in the modern Indian cultural domain. His nature to explore the various materials and mediums allowed him to make a prolific body of work in different mediums. Bose's sketches captures lived life, people and animals, in the settings with the context and references, with fine rhythmic lines be it pencil, brush, or any medium. Most of his sketches have a strong tendency of documentation and show a continuous involvement with the surroundings that the artist was present in. There are many works that he sketched from his observations of nature in watercolours. This painting belongs to the series of sketches of the Sun.

This painting was purchased from the collection of Shri Biswaroop Bose and Smt. Nivedita Bose, children of Nandalal Bose.

artworks.title: The Sun
artworks.description: Nandalal's work depicts changing landscapes, portraits of people, sketches from life and places at the time of changing outlook in the modern Indian cultural domain. His nature to explore the various materials and mediums allowed him to make a prolific body of work in different mediums. Bose's sketches captures lived life, people and animals, in the settings with the context and references, with fine rhythmic lines be it pencil, brush, or any medium. Most of his sketches have a strong tendency of documentation and show a continuous involvement with the surroundings that the artist was present in. There are many works that he sketched from his observations of nature in watercolours. This painting belongs to the series of works titled as the Sun.

artworks.description: Nandalal's work depicts changing landscapes, portraits of people, sketches from life and places at the time of changing outlook in the modern Indian cultural domain. His nature to explore the various materials and mediums allowed him to make a prolific body of work in different mediums. Bose's sketches captures lived life, people and animals, in the settings with the context and references, with fine rhythmic lines be it pencil, brush, or any medium. Most of his sketches have a strong tendency of documentation and show a continuous involvement with the surroundings that the artist was present in. There are many works that he sketched from his observations of nature in watercolours. This watercolour is amongst the series of Mountains.

artworks.title: Mountains
artworks.medium: Black & white watercolour on sumi paper
artworks.description: A. Ramachandran in the book, 'Rhythms of India: The Art of Nandalal Bose' writes, "After retirement from a long service of teaching (and even though his mobility was restricted due to less than robust health), Nandalal settled down in his home studio for a retrospective examination of the images he had stored in his mind over long years. As if he were in fact writing his autobiography, Nandalal returned to the early years of his life to take stock of the scenes and images that he had collected, and he continued to spontaneously record human figures, animals, mountain ranges, hills, rivers, waterfalls, landscapes, flights of birds, trees, plants, insects, etc, on mounted handmade papers using only ink and brush."

The subject here being 'Mountains' executed from his memory and experiences. These compositions were stripped to the bare minimum where only a few strokes of ink were employed to create natural forms in an effortless approach. This painting was purchased from the collection of Shri Biswaroop Bose and Smt. Nivedita Bose, children of Nandalal Bose.

artworks.title: Mountains
artworks.description: Nandalal's work depicts changing landscapes, portraits of people, sketches from life and places at the time of changing outlook in the modern Indian cultural domain. His nature to explore the various materials and mediums allowed him to make a prolific body of work in different mediums. Bose's sketches captures lived life, people and animals, in the settings with the context and references, with fine rhythmic lines be it pencil, brush, or any medium. Most of his sketches have a strong tendency of documentation and show a continuous involvement with the surroundings that the artist was present in. There are many works that he sketched from his observations of nature in watercolours. The watercolour rendering is from the series of studies of Mountains.

artworks.title: Mountains
artworks.medium: Black & white watercolour on sumi paper
artworks.description: This painting belongs to a series of monochromatic ink and watercolour paintings inspired by the Sumi-e Japanese technique the artist employed in the last phase of his life. The subject here being the 'Mountains' executed from his memory and experiences. R. Siva Kumar in the book, 'Rhythms of India: The Art of Nandalal Bose' writes, Freed of the distracting noises of nation and tradition, these are quiter images. Here the artist becomes the marks his tool leaves on the paper, and the world becomes the weightless imprint of touch and space it leaves on his consciousness." This painting was purchased from the collection of Shri Biswaroop Bose and Smt. Nivedita Bose, children of Nandalal Bose.

artworks.title: Hills
artworks.description: Nandalal's work depicts changing landscapes, portraits of people, sketches from life and places at the time of changing outlook in the modern Indian cultural domain. His nature to explore the various materials and mediums allowed him to make a prolific body of work in different mediums. Bose's sketches captures lived life, people and animals, in the settings with the context and references, with fine rhythmic lines be it pencil, brush, or any medium. Most of his sketches have a strong tendency of documentation and show a continuous involvement with the surroundings that the artist was present in. There are many works that he sketched from his observations of nature in watercolours. This sketch is amongst the series of sketches of hills.

artworks.title: Hills
artworks.description: Nandalal's work depicts changing landscapes, portraits of people, sketches from life and places at the time of changing outlook in the modern Indian cultural domain. His nature to explore the various materials and mediums allowed him to make a prolific body of work in different mediums. Bose's sketches captures lived life, people and animals, in the settings with the context and references, with fine rhythmic lines be it pencil, brush, or any medium. Most of his sketches have a strong tendency of documentation and show a continuous involvement with the surroundings that the artist was present in. There are many works that he sketched from his observations of nature in watercolours. This sketch is amongst the series of sketches of hills.

artworks.title: Hills
artworks.description: Nandalal's work depicts changing landscapes, portraits of people, sketches from life and places at the time of changing outlook in the modern Indian cultural domain. His nature to explore the various materials and mediums allowed him to make a prolific body of work in different mediums. Bose's sketches captures lived life, people and animals, in the settings with the context and references, with fine rhythmic lines be it pencil, brush, or any medium. Most of his sketches have a strong tendency of documentation and show a continuous involvement with the surroundings that the artist was present in. There are many works that he sketched from his observations of nature in watercolours. This sketch is amongst the series of sketches of hills.

artworks.title: The Lotus
artworks.description: Nandalal's work depicts changing landscapes, portraits of people, sketches from life and places at the time of changing outlook in the modern Indian cultural domain. His nature to explore the various materials and mediums allowed him to make a prolific body of work in different mediums. Bose's sketches captures lived life, people and animals, in the settings with the context and references, with fine rhythmic lines be it pencil, brush, or any medium. Most of his sketches have a strong tendency of documentation and show a continuous involvement with the surroundings that the artist was present in. There are many works that he sketched from his observations of nature in watercolours. This watercolour rendering shows a study of lotus flower on Sumi paper.

artworks.title: The Bamboo Trees
artworks.description: Nandalal's work depicts changing landscapes, portraits of people, sketches from life and places at the time of changing outlook in the modern Indian cultural domain. His nature to explore the various materials and mediums allowed him to make a prolific body of work in different mediums. Bose's sketches captures lived life, people and animals, in the settings with the context and references, with fine rhythmic lines be it pencil, brush, or any medium. Most of his sketches have a strong tendency of documentation and show a continuous involvement with the surroundings that the artist was present in. He sketched from his observations of nature in watercolours. This water colour rendering shows the sketch of Bamboo trees. He sketched from his observations of nature in watercolours. This water colour rendering shows the sketch of Bamboo trees.

The subject here being 'Wild Animals' executed from his memory and experiences. A. Ramachandran in the book, 'Rhythms of India: The Art of Nandalal Bose' writes, "After retirement from a long service of teaching (and even though his mobility was restricted due to less than robust health), Nandalal settled down in his home studio for a retrospective examination of the images he had stored in his mind over long years. As if he were in fact writing his autobiography, Nandalal returned to the early years of his life to take stock of the scenes and images that he had collected, and he continued to spontaneously record human figures, animals, mountain ranges, hills, rivers, waterfalls, landscapes, flights of birds, trees, plants, insects, etc, on mounted handmade papers using only ink and brush."

Ramachandran in the book, 'Rhythms of India: The Art of Nandalal Bose' writes, "After retirement from a long service of teaching (and even though his mobility was restricted due to less than robust health), Nandalal settled down in his home studio for a retrospective examination of the images he had stored in his mind over long years. artworks.title: Playing Musical Instruments

His nature to explore the various materials and mediums allowed him to make a prolific body of work in different mediums. Bose's sketches captures lived life, people and animals, in the settings with the context and references, with fine rhythmic lines be it pencil, brush, or any medium. This sketch with watercolour on paper depicts the villagers playing musical instruments.

artworks.title: Album No. - 4 (Landscapes)
artworks.description: Nandalal preferred drawing from life, often sketching outdoors with the subject being life, nature studies, landscapes, figure drawings, animals. Often the sketches were small in scale although invigorating with the rich detailing of the artist's observations, experiences and sojourns to various places. In this pencil drawing the artist has captured the scenic landscape with the use of spontaneous lines. The water in the river gracefully meanders between the distinctively drawn bushes and leaves, whereas a horizon in the deep background is handled in soft curls with pencil.

artworks.title: Album No. - 4 (Landscapes)
artworks.description: Nandalal had a strong affinity for sketching and drawing, instantly recording in the post card sized papers his subjects from the surrounding environs, people in their everyday life, animals, flora and fauna or anything that he found fascinating. The drawings complete in themselves were his vivid observations of the characteristics and attributes of subjects chosen from his immediate surroundings. The present pencil drawing is a port scene with boats docked together, an enormous mill with its towers in the vicinity and flocks of seagulls in the air. The artist has amalgamated the elements of nature with that of the industrial area. Nandalal himself in his book, 'On Art' has written- "Nature is life itself and teeming always with infinite variety; it is in her that the artist always renews his experience and finds an unceasing flow of inspiration."

metadata.inscription: Signed and dated 'Nanda (Bengali), 3.10.30 (English)' along the right margin of the painting. The painting has an inscription which reads, 'Raj Singh Mills' in English at the right bottom corner with pencil.

artworks.title: Album No. - 4 (Landscapes)
artworks.description: Nandalal had firm belief that for the creation of art an intimate understanding of the nature and its ways is imperative. His smaller sketches are testimony of Nandalal's keenness to observe and his empathy for the environment in which he lived.This sketch was probably made during the artist's visit to the coast of Orissa. Nandalal has made careful observation for his numerous sketches depicting the landscape, seascapes and the local tribes, particularly the Nulia tribes. The sketch is executed with quick and spontaneous brush strokes and is one of many examples of Nandalal's acute observation of his surroundings. The deep perspective and human forms in the above landscape painting is created with simple line formations.

metadata.inscription: Signed and dated 'Nanda (Bengali), 16.10.32 (English) at the bottom of the painting with pencil. The painting also has an inscription which reads, 'Puri' with pencil.

artworks.title: Album No. - 4 (Landscapes)
artworks.description: Nandalal is known to have fervently sketched on postcard sized papers mostly using ink and brush, recording his surroundings. His small sketches vastly vary in detailing, some drawn quickly with just a few lines, others executed with more elaborate characteristics from an analytical perspective. Bansberi is a small town and a municipality in Hooghly district in the state of West Bengal, it is located in the West Bank of the Hoogly river. This work, is among the many sketches Nandalal made in Bansberi. Nandalal made quick sketches of people boarding the boats near the shore and would usually finish the sketch with a deep horizon in the background.

metadata.inscription: Dated '30.12.34' and inscribed 'Bansberi'in English at the left bottom corner of the painting with pencil.

artworks.title: Album No. - 4 (Landscapes)
artworks.description: Nandalal is known to have fervently sketched on postcard sized papers mostly using ink and brush, recording his surroundings. His small sketches vastly vary in detailing, some drawn quickly with just a few lines, others executed with more elaborate characteristics from an analytical perspective. The artist made the sketch during one of his travels to the the coast of Orissa, carefully observing the landscape, seascapes and the local tribes of the region. In his book, 'Nandalal Bose - The Doyen of Indian Art', Dinkar Kaushik observes that, 'Nandalal's respect for the infinite variety of nature was one of the major factors that forced him out of the world of myths and legends'.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 11 (A Portrait Study)
artworks.description: This postcard sketch shows a man in profile rendered with thick and fluid lines defining the contours of his form. The amalgamation of thick and calligraphic strokes lends a stern yet soft look to the face. Jaya Appasamy in her article, 'Nandalal- Master Draughtsman' writes of these sketches, "The drawings on postcards have a spontaneity and brevity not seen in more formal works. They exist as evidence of the artist's unceasing desire to master visual data."

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 11 (A Portrait Study)
artworks.description: Nandalal had firm belief that for the creation of art an intimate understanding of the nature and its ways is imperative. His smaller sketches are testimony of Nandalal's keenness to observe and his empathy for the environment in which he lived. The above drawing is a pencil portrait of a turbaned man. Dinkar Kowshik in his article 'Drawings and Sketches of Nandalal in the book titled "Nandalal Bose - A collection of Essays" has elucidated about the sketches of Nandalal in the words, "Nandalal's sketches in fact provide a moving record of a humble life and natural environment in which he lived. These are not in any way preliminary studies for his larger finished compositions in black and white or in colour. They are finished and self-contained in themselves like a Japanese 'Haiku'. Their spacing, their distribution of black and white, their linear or tonal accents and the signature all form a part of a single unit."

This particular postcard sketch depicts a dog resting, rendered with thick, fluid lines defining the contours of his form. Jaya Appasamy in her article, 'Nandalal- Master Draughtsman' writes of these sketches, "The drawings on postcards have a spontaneity and brevity not seen in more formal works. They exist as evidence of the artist's unceasing desire to master visual data."

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' and dated '18.4.1932' along the lower margin of the sketch. There is an inscription in Bengali that can be translated as 'From today summer vacation has started and we all have come to stay here with your mother, Gora, Gori, Bani, Kumari'.

artworks.title: Album No. 12 (A Landscape)
artworks.description: Nandalal preferred drawing from life, often sketching outdoors with the subject being life, nature studies, landscapes, figure drawings, and animals. Often the sketches were small in scale although invigorating with the rich detailing of the artist's observations, experiences and sojourns to various places. The above illustration by the artist depicts a railway track, lined with palm trees on the side. The rendering of the track and the trees are done by the use of dark, bold strokes, creating an interplay of diagonal and vertical lines.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali in the bottom-left corner of the sketch. There is also an indecipherable inscription.

artworks.title: Album No. 12 (A Landscape)
artworks.description: The above illustration by Nandalal is a perceptible representation of the Manikarnika Ghat, one of the ghats of Benaras. In the sketch, the artist has delineated architectural structures and human figures with thick, fluid lines conveying the bustle at the river bank.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nandalal Bose' and dated '13.4.35' in Bengali along the left margin of the sketch with pen and black ink. There is also an inscription in Bengali that can be translated as, 'Manikarnika Ghat'.

artworks.title: Album No. 12 (A Landscape)
artworks.description: Nandalal is known to have fervently sketched on postcard sized papers mostly using ink and brush, recording his surroundings. He evolved his visual language by studying the art practices and traditions not only of India but also those of other nations. The above sketch is a perceptible representation of the bank of river Triveni. The forms are rendered with linear outlines which are further blurred and.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and Dated '29.12.34' in the bottom-left corner with pen and black ink. There is also an inscription in English that can be read as, 'Triveni'.

artworks.title: Album No. 12 (A Landscape)
artworks.description: Nandalal had a strong affinity for sketching and drawing, instantly recording in the post card sized papers, his subjects from the surrounding environs, anything that he found fascinating. The drawings complete in themselves were his vivid observations of the characteristics and attributes of subjects. The above monochrome illustration depicts, rice paddies hung on wooden poles to dry. It has been swiftly executed by soft smudged, coarse pencil strokes suggesting the contours of the paddies amidst a harvested land.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nandalal Bose' in Bengali in the bottom-right corner with pencil. There is also an inscription in English that can be read as, 'Santineketan'.

artworks.title: Album No. 12 (A Landscape)
artworks.description: Nandalal had a strong affinity for sketching, his subjects being the surrounding environs, people in their everyday life or anything that he found fascinating. In the above monochrome illustration, he has depicted a village scene where three men are making jaggery from the nectar of date palm. The use of bold, sharp lines for the contours and soft strokes for the textures of the forms adds vitality to the composition.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' and dated '4.11.33' in English in the bottom-right corner of the sketch.

artworks.title: Album No. 12 (A Landscape)
artworks.description: This sketch by Nandalal depicts a family walking along a path amidst a rural setting suggested by the hut and trees in the background. The various forms in the illustration, are sketched with the use of black, bold lines. The stark silhouettes are filled with soft, smudged strokes to lend texture to these forms, adding life and vitality to the sketch.

metadata.inscription: There is an indecipherable inscription in the bottom-right corner of the sketch.

artworks.title: Album No. 12 (A Landscape)
artworks.description: This is another monochrome illustration by Nandalal Bose, of the river Triveni, sketched in 1935. The sketch depicts a boat along the river shore. The background is depicted with dark, spiral lines which suggest the depth in the image, in contrast to which Nandalal has used calligraphic lines to depict the river.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '1.1.35' in the bottom-right corner of the postcard with pencil.

artworks.title: Album No. 12 (A Landscape)

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' and dated '7.4.35' in Bengali along the lower margin of the postcard with pencil. There is also an inscription in English that can be read as, 'Triveni'.

artworks.title: Album No. 12 (A Landscape)

artworks.title: Album No. 12 (A Landscape)
artworks.description: Nandalal is known to have fervently sketched on postcard sized papers, recording his surroundings. In the sketch above, he has depicted a cluster of high rise buildings with narrow lanes. The artist has used dark, firm lines to depict the crowded architectural structures interspersed with human figures.

metadata.inscription: There is an inscription in Bengali that can be translated as, 'Bengali Tolla, August Kunj' along the upper margin.

artworks.title: Album No. 13 (A Landscape)
artworks.description: This postcard sketch renders an image of fishermen in boats on a large expanse of water, suggested with bold, linear lines. Nandalal harmonises nature and human beings by using simple rhythmic lines for both, the water and the boats.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '1.11.1930' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is another inscription in English that reads, "Rajmehal", referring to the place it was sketched at.

artworks.title: Album No. 12 (A Landscape)
artworks.description: Nandalal had a strong affinity for sketching and used a variety of lines to create graphic representations of his visual experiences. His sketches vastly vary in detailing, some drawn quickly with just a few lines, others executed with more elaborate characteristics from an analytical perspective. The above monochrome sketch depicts an architectural structure rendered using dark, sharp lines. The entire composition is covered with cross hatching and stippling which gives the appearance of a veil covering the image.

artworks.title: Album No. 13 (A Landscape)
artworks.description: Nandalal's drawings on postcards are spontaneous done either with pen or a brush, the aim was simply to capture the subject and the moment. In this sketch, Nandalal has depicted a landscape with a boat in the foreground, rendered in dark loose angular brush strokes. He has studied the forms in a minimalist manner, sparing much detail in the image.

metadata.inscription: Dated '26.10.1930' in English and signed 'Nanda' in Bengali along the lower margin of the sketch.

artworks.title: Album No. 13 (A Study of Tagore)
artworks.description: This postcard sketch shows a portrait of Rabindranath Tagore rendered with ink in the dry brush technique. Nandalal carefully brings out the facial features with tonal variations of ink. metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '3.11.30' in English. There is another inscription in English that reads, "Rajmehal", referring to the place it was sketched at.

artworks.title: Album No. 13 (A Landscape)

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '3.11.30' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '2.11.30' in English below the sketch. There is another inscription in English that reads, "Rajmehal", referring to the place it was sketched at.

artworks.title: Album No. 13 (A Portrait Study)
artworks.description: The postcard sketch shows the portrait of a young bearded man rendered with ink in the dry brush technique using thick and dark strokes. The strong and rough brushwork lends a rugged look to the face.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali below the sketch. There is another inscription in English that reads, "Rajmehal, Singhidalan" and the sketch is dated '13.11.1930'.

artworks.title: Album No. 14 (A Sketch)
artworks.description: Nandalal understood the significance of the use of lines and experimented frequently in their execution from fine lines to being thick contouring lines. This sketch by him is a portrait of an old man. The fluid handling of the line and the dark ink strokes suggest the contours of the face, highlighting the facial features while the rest of the figure has been rendered in swift, short strokes.

metadata.inscription: Dated '18.1.35' in English and signed 'Nanda' in Bengali along the left margin of the sketch. The sketch also has an inscription in English which reads 'Buxur (Buxar)' below the signature.

artworks.title: Album No. 13 (A Portrait Study)

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '1.11.30' in English below the sketch.

artworks.title: Album No. 13 (A Sketch of a Worker)

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali at the top and bottom left corners. There is another inscription in English that reads, "Rajmehal" referring to the place it was sketched at and is dated '3.11.30'.

artworks.title: Album No. 15 (A Dancing Mudra)
artworks.description: Nandalal had a strong affinity for sketching, avidly recording the flora and fauna, the people of the place, their dress, their carriages, the headdress, the landscape, the festivals, and the architecture. In his pencil sketches, Nandalal has experimented with the use of lines to add texture, vigour and life to his sketches. artworks.description: This is another one of Nandalal's quickly executed sketches. Here the artist renders the form of a woman dressed in traditional Northern Indian attire of a long skirt and a drape that covers the head.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 17
artworks.description: In this image, Nandalal has quickly sketched the form of a woman seated on the ground. Eminent artist A. Ramachandran in the book, 'Rhythms of India: The Art of Nandalal Bose' has made the following observation about Nandalal's drawings and sketches, ?He made quick graphic impressions, often simplifying them to just few lines as he sought to understand the inherent structure of what he was seeing. At times he recorded objects in a more analytical way, while at others he transformed them into visual codes of pattern.?

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 23
artworks.description: This postcard shows a herd of donkeys guided by a female herder at the construction site of the Congress convention in Faizpur (Maharashtra). The light shading and thick outlines define the contours of the organic figures. About the depiction of animals, Nandalal in his book, 'Vision and Creation' wrote, "Each creature has a basic spinal rhythm following its characteristic nature. A certain kind of movement or rhythm finds expression in the body of an animal following each emotional impulse, and this becomes for us its characteristic gesture. These body rhythms are based on the structure of the backbone, and this is seen most clearly from the side. The body's mass, structure and volume should be studied in relation with this life rhythm; it controls them and, in turn, is controlled by them."

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '8.12.36' in English in the top-left corner of the sketch, with an inscription which reads, 'Faizpur'. There is another inscription in Bengali along the lower margin which reads, "Construction work in progress".

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 23
artworks.description: In this postcard Nandalal has rendered the site where he and his students set up camp in Faizpur (Maharashtra) to study his subjects closely. The artist carefully studied the structure and characteristics of trees wherever he went. Here he accentuates the tree with heavy lines and varying strokes. In his book, 'Vision and Creation' he writes, "A tree grows upward; it is driven by a singular urge to spread towards the sky- trunk, branch and leaf. The trunk is like the tree's backbone; so its characteristic rhythm has to be drawn first; then its main structure with branch and twig; and finally, the total image with its bunches of leaves and shoots."

metadata.inscription: Dated '31.12.36' in Bengali in the bottom-left corner of the sketch. There is another inscription in Bengali that reads, 'Faizpur'.

Nandalal has marked himself within the drawing with a cross and signed 'Nanda', sitting on the ground next to the podium on the right.

Here he has sketched the figure of a person working at the construction site of the Congress convention at Tilak nagar, Faizpur (Maharashtra) in 1937. Nandalal renders the sketch in short, sharp strokes, defining the contours of his sunken face and lean body, delineated in an illustrative manner.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '28.11.36' along the right margin of the sketch. The inscription on the left hand side reads, 'Faizpur, Tilak Nagar, E. Khandesh', in English. There are two other inscriptions in Bengali, that read, "Medhi master" and, "He is helping to construct the gate."

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 23
artworks.description: Nandalal employed artisans and craftsmen from Faizpur (Maharashtra) during the Congress convention in 1937, to construct gates and temporary structures using only local materials, such as bamboo, wood, and hay. This postcard shows, in light and fluid outlines, the podium among the decorated bamboo staves at the site. Nandalal applies Sino-Japanese brushwork techniques and enhances the sketch by making use of the translucent quality of ink to its fullest.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 25

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 25
artworks.description: This postcard sketch portrays a rath yatra or Chariot festival, a Hindu festival, wherein deities are transported in grandly decorated chariots, from their resident temple to a distant temple and brought back after nine days. Nandalal renders the Vithalnagar procession in clean and thick lines in an illustrative manner.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '30.1.38' along the bottom of the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, "Vithalnagar",(a small settlement near Haripura in Gujarat, India). There is another inscription in Bengali, that roughly reads, "villagers watching the chariot festival."

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 25

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 25

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 25

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No 26
artworks.description: This postcard shows parts of a column as rendered in Indian temple architecture. The relaxed manner of drawing shows Nandalal's impulse to quickly record the pillar in its original form and enrich his knowledge of design and ornamental work.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 26
artworks.description: The postcard shows flower inspired motifs with different linear patterns in simple designs. The markings show the colours red, black and yellow to be filled within the motifs. This design was probably created for use in an 'alpona', a decorative design used on floors during festivals and auspicious occasions in Bengal.

metadata.inscription: The markings over the motifs read, 'Red', 'Black' and 'Yellow' in Bengali. There is another inscription in Bengali on the bottom which reads, 'Designs to fill in petals.'

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No 26
artworks.description: In this postcard Nandalal has amalgamated distinct geometric and organic patterns to form a variety of designs. This probably is a template for an alpana design (floor and wall decorations made with rice-paste on special occasions and festivals). Nandalal encouraged his students at Santiniketan to participate in alpana making as it was a collective participatory ritual.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali in the top-right corner of the sketch.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 26
artworks.description: This postcard shows a sketch of a lotus scroll, probably from the base, plinth or column of a temple. It is a quick observation study with pencil. Nandalal in his book 'On Art' writes, "The form of lotus gets modified according to the material the artist has to work upon, and hence the remarkable variety of its design."

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 26

The sketch portrays Nandalal's impulse to imitate the motif in its original form to enrich his knowledge of design and ornamental work.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali in the top-left corner of the sketch.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No 26

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali on the top left corner. The other markings over the postcard read, 'Red' and 'Black' in Bengali.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 26

The combination of soft curving lines and sharp cutting outlines blended in a single form here, strikes a balance in the design. Nandalal in his book 'On Art' writes, ''The ornamental design as compared with nature is far more simple and abstract.''

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 41
artworks.description: Nandalal is known to have depicted profusely the environs and surroundings of Santiniketan, where he lived and taught. In this postcard sized sketch, he has rendered a shepherd tugging at his load- bearing horse amidst a rural landscape. Using large curvilinear strokes in the outlines, the figures have been lent solidity and volume, while minimal lines convey expressions of hardship, both human and animal.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 41
artworks.description: Nandalal sketched fervently, the environs of Santiniketan in Bengal, where he lived and taught and would keenly record aspects of rural life from the region. This sketch, the first in a series of three sketches of hens in the album, depicts a mother hen followed by two younger ones tottering around her. The strokes are quick and smudged, conveying the hurried movement of the birds.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated 14.11.1941 in English with black crayon in the bottom-right corner.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 41
artworks.description: Nandalal is known to have fervently sketched on postcard sized papers mostly using ink and brush, recording his surroundings. His small sketches vastly vary in detailing, some drawn quickly with just a few lines, others executed with more elaborate characteristics from an analytical perspective. In this second sketch of the series, Nandalal has depicted a mother hen surrounded by her young chicks. Without demarcating outlines, he has rendered the forms in scribbles done swiftly and loosely.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 41
artworks.description: This is another one of Nandalal's quick sketches. Characterised by their loose strokes and outlines, their purpose is to serve as studies of poses as well as an exploration of forms at their most basic. Rendered here in watercolour is the image of a herd of bulls seated amidst village hutments. Such scenes of rural life were among the most recurring themes in Nandalal's works.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated 8.3.1943 in English in the bottom- left corner with brush and black watercolour.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 41
artworks.description: In this sketch of a dog, Nandalal has captured the details of its anatomy and the expression of hunger writ on its face, in its eyes and salivating tongue. In short, precise strokes, he has made evident the emaciated figure of the animal and its heightened state of alertness. In his book, 'On Art', Nandalal elaborates on an artistic understanding of anatomy thus, ''To acquire right knowledge and perception one should study men and animals when they are on the move or are active : when one can note in action the how and wherefore of the body's muscles, tendons and joints.''

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated 2.12.1942 in English with pen and black ink along the left margin of the painting.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 41
artworks.description: This postcard sized drawing of a hen-keeper, clasping a hen in each hand while another flutters behind him, is not only a study of the animal form but a vivid exploration of the rustic male body. In clear, defined outlines Nandalal has brought out both, the helplessness of the birds and the resolve of the keeper in taming them. This is the third and last in a series of three sketches on hens in this album.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 41

metadata.inscription: Dated '31.12.1942' in English and signed 'Nanda' in Bengali along the left margin of the sketch. The sketch bears an inscription in Bengali that can be translated as, 'Samantha Dahu, Tano Danga' (referring to the place ).

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 41
artworks.description: This is another one of Nandalal's quickly executed sketches. Characterised by their loose strokes and outlines, their purpose is to serve as studies of poses as well as an exploration of forms at their most basic. Stripping it of superfluous detail, only the bare minimum remains. This particular sketch shows a lean, reclining cow from behind. Its elongated back and bent head lends it grace and a pensive mood.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated 26.3.1943 in English with pencil along the right margin of the drawing.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 41
artworks.description: Nandalal is known to have depicted fervently, the environs and surroundings of Santiniketan in Bengal where he lived and taught. Another in the series of animal studies, this sketch by Nandalal shows an emaciated female goat chewing on grass. The broad strokes used stress on the outlines and the form rather than on detail. It can also be seen that before executing the sketch in ink, Nandalal drew it with loose strokes of a pencil, still visible under the finished work.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 41
artworks.description: In this sketch Nandalal has depicted a male goat from the region of Goalpara (as the inscription indicates), a district in Assam along the Brahmaputra river, on one of his travels in the state. While being faithful to its form, he has used short, brief strokes to bring out the texture of its fur and lend it tangibility. The upward and downward flow of the strokes guides the viewer's eye to glide along the image effortlessly.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated 28.9.1942 in English with pen and black ink in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. Along the bottom-centre is another inscription in English that reads, 'Goalpara', referring to the place it was sketched at.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 41

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 41
artworks.description: This sketch of a donkey grazing is another of Nandalal's animal drawings. Here he explores not only the form but also the emotion of the animal. An empty expression in the eyes and inertia in its body language, as depicted by the artist, convey its emotional state. In his book, 'On Art', Nandalal elaborates on an artistic understanding of anatomy thus, "To acquire right knowledge and perception one should study men and animals when they are on the move or are active : when one can note in action the how and wherefore of the body's muscles, tendons and joints."

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 41
artworks.description: This image, of a flock of five storks in a swampy area is a quick sketch executed with watercolour and broad, sweeping strokes by the artist. The intent not being to illustrate detail, but to capture a fleeting moment with the birds in water, in a minimalist manner. The suggestions of ripples and the shadows in them gives it an ephemeral quality. The slight variations in their expressions lend variety to the otherwise identical and uniform poses.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 41
artworks.description: Nandlal preferred drawing from life, often sketching outdoors with the subject being nature studies, landscapes, figure drawings and animals. Often the sketches were small in scale although invigorating with the rich detailing of the artist's observations, experiences and sojourns to various places. These interactions between the different forms of nature characterise a large part of Nandlal?s artistic corpus. In this sketch, he has rendered the frontal profile of a cow's head, its expression vividly captured in brief, quick strokes.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 41
artworks.medium: Pen and ink and pencil on postcard
artworks.description: Nandalal is known to have fervently sketched the environs and surroundings of Santiniketan in Bengal, India where he lived and taught. This particular sketch is the study of a sheep in movement while it grazes on wisps of grass. Along the right margin are three simple line drawings that explore variations of the same pose and make evident the artist's expertise on capturing a dynamic moment. Nandalal's artistic corpus is replete with such nature studies that explore flora and fauna in their habitats.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated 2.12.1942 in English with pen and black ink in the bottom-right corner.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 41
artworks.description: Nandalal Bose was indefatigable in his sketching routines which formed an adjunct part of his daily life. Making instantaneous visual records of anything amusing happening in his surroundings or of social events, or observing the demeanour and mannerisms of people, cattle and observing intently the ways of nature was inspiring and a source of delight for Nandalal. In keeping with his other studies of insects, the artist has here rendered a drawing of a cockroach. He has meticulously captured every detail of the roach in precise strokes emphasising its structure and nimbleness.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 41

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 42
artworks.description: In this postcard sized work, Nandalal has sketched an elephant in soft, loose strokes. The idea being to emphasise outlines and figurative accuracy, without indulging in textural details. In his book, 'On Art', Nandalal elaborates on the artistic concept of anatomy thus, "To acquire right knowledge and perception one should study men and animals when they are on the move or are active: when one can note in action the how and wherefore of the body's muscles, tendons and joints."

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 43
artworks.description: Here Nandalal has rendered a view of Darjeeling, which is located in the foothills of the Himalayas in northern Bengal. He has represented the mountains covered with snow and mist. This painting is one of the landscapes in the monochrome ink wash technique, which shows his inclination towards Chinese and Japanese painting traditions. The wide expanses of snow in the image recall his statement on landscape painting in his book, 'Vision and Creation', ''Landscapes can be painted in the manner of seas, with wavy heaps of stone and earth.''

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '19.05.45' in English vertically along the bottom right corner of the painting with black ink and brush.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 43
artworks.description: Nandalal recorded various scenes of nature and everyday life wherever he travelled. This drawing is also one of the works which depicts the streets of Darjeeling. Here, a woman can be seen carrying a child on her back and ascending a flight of stairs that have been rendered with thick brush strokes. He has also, as a template, roughly scribbled the form of the woman in blue colour on the top-right corner; the aim was simply to capture the subject in a brief moment. Most of his sketches are in monochrome but here he has used red and ochre colours to add some detail.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '11.05.45' in English vertically along the top-right corner of the image with black ink and brush. There is an inscription along the right margin in English that reads, 'Darjeeling'.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 43
artworks.description: In this landscape painting, Nandalal has utilised the tonal variations of black ink with water for creating a recognisable effect of mountains covered with snow and fog. He has also depicted some vegetation on the peaks of the mountains and at the lower left foreground with ink patches in a darker tone. R. Siva Kumar in the book, 'Rhythms of India: The Art of Nandalal Bose' writes of the artist, "In spite of specificities of location, not all of his drawings were done on location...he gave to works done in the studio the same vividness found in his studies done directly from nature."

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '17.05.45' in English in the left corner of the painting with brush and black ink.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 43
artworks.description: The techniques of harmonious dilution of colours Nandalal acquired from the arts of the Far East. In this painting of the hills of Darjeeling, he has utilised the tonal variations of black ink with water for creating a recognisable effect of mountains covered with snow. He has also depicted trees and vegetation peculiar to a hill terrain at the lower left foreground with ink patches.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '11.05.45' in English in the bottom left corner with brush and black ink. There is another inscription in Bengali that reads, 'Darjeeling'.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 43
artworks.description: Nandalal had a strong affinity for sketching and drawing, his subjects being the surrounding environs, life of people and their everyday chores. His smaller sketches are testimony of Nandalal's keenness to observe and his empathy for the environment in which he lived. Here he has represented a scene of Darjeeling, the hills of the region shrouded in mist. He has utilised the texture of the paper as part of the work by smudging charcoal on it and creating varied tones of gray that lend an impression of haze in the environment.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '09.05.45' in English horizontally along the left margin of the painting with black ink and brush. There is another inscription in Bengali that can be translated as 'Darjeeling'.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 43
artworks.description: Nandalal was greatly influenced by the Far Eastern painting traditions. He has painted many of his landscapes in this style. Here he has rendered a mountainscape covered in mist and haze. He has deftly used dark patches of ink to suggest vegetation on the hill, offset by the light grey patches of mist. As Jaya Appasamy writes in her essay, 'Nandalal - Master Draughtsman' in the book 'Nandalal Bose (1882-1966) Centenary Exhibition', ''In the drawings the background is left bare and the brush strokes, dark and light build up a tonal picture. The unfinished wet quality of some of these works is part of the idiom.''

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '17.05.45' in English horizontally at the left corner of the painting with brush and black ink.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 43

In this painting he has employed the amorphous ink wash technique in the background with a little tint of black and some grey patches to give an impression of the mountain. Jaya Appasamy in her essay, 'Nandalal - Master Draughtsmen' in the book, 'Nandalal Bose (1882-1966) Centenary Exhibition' elucidates, "In the drawings the background is left bare and the brush strokes, dark and light build up a tonal picture. artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 43
artworks.description: This a drawing by Nandalal painted probably on one of his visits to Darjeeling. It depicts a pillar with a dragon figure intertwined around it, portraying the Buddhist guardian deity, Mahakal, as the inscription suggests. This style draws from the tradition of Thangka painting, which is still alive within the monastic communities of Tibetan Buddhism.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 43
artworks.description: Nandalal had a strong affinity for sketching and drawing, instantly recording on post card sized paper scenes of nature and everyday life. This drawing is also one of the works painted from the streets of Darjeeling. Here a lady is seated at the counter of a hotel, cooking on a traditional stove. The drawing has been created with linear strokes of pen, using curved lines only to give volume to the body of the lady and the pots and utensils kept near her. His quick strokes were simply aimed to capture the subject in a brief moment.

This painting is a landscape in the monochrome ink wash technique, which is associated with specific Chinese and Japanese landscape traditions. artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 43

Painting in the same style, here he has rendered the backdrop in light tints of black and added grey patches to give an impression of black clouds above the mountains. As Jaya Appasamy writes in her essay, 'Nandalal- Master Draughtsman' in the book 'Nandalal Bose (1882-1966) Centenary Exhibition', ''In the drawings the background is left bare and the brush strokes, dark and light build up a tonal picture. In his pencil sketches he has experimented with the use of lines to add texture, vigour and life to his sketches. This quick sketch depicts a gardener trimming plants. The fluid, smudged strokes delineate the fine contours of the robust male form.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 44
artworks.description: The blurring of the linear outlines of the figures and the harmonious dilution of the colours were techniques Nandalal acquired from the arts of the Far East. The technique of modulating the ink tones from darker through lighter to obtain a variety of shadings from near white, through grey tones to blacks was mastered and implemented in several of his works. This particular sketch executed with quick strokes is one of many examples of Nandalal's acute observation of his surroundings. In the above village scene, the perceptible representation of the trees with their ridged surfaces is executed with a range of brush strokes.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 45

Nandalal is known to have fervently sketched on postcard sized papers mostly using either pencil or ink and brush, recording his surroundings. His small sketches vastly vary in detailing, some drawn quickly with just a few lines, others executed with more elaborate characteristics from an analytical perspective. His search for newer forms of expression and his inner urge to constantly innovate is well reflected in the multiple postcards in the collection of the museum which portray the artist's visual experiences of flora fauna, the people, their attires, life in rural villages, the landscapes. Dinkar Kowshik in his article 'Drawings and Sketches of Nandalal in the book, "Nandalal Bose - A collection of Essays" has written of Nandalal's sketches and drawings - "Much of his (Nandalal) strength and sensitive wealth finds expression in the spontaneity of his sketches. They are a veritable treasure of shrewd observation, powerful calligraphy, psychological insight, rich sallies of humour and emphatic portrayal of the flora and fauna."

artworks.description: The above postcard illustrates a sketch of the bird- the Indian Roller, commonly known as the 'Neelkanth', meaning 'blue throat' in India. The above sketch is presumably either a preliminary sketch or a study, where the artist has marked and labelled the bird with specific colours and shades. With the use of subtle lines and shades, Nandalal adds grace and spirit to the form of the bird. Nandalal Bose in his book, 'On Art' has written- "Nature is life itself and teeming always with infinite variety; it is in her that the artist always renews his experience and finds an unceasing flow of inspiration."

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 45
artworks.description: Nandalal was indefatigable in his sketching routines which formed an adjunct part of his daily life. Making instantaneous visual records of anything amusing happening in his surroundings or of social events, or observing the demeanour and mannerisms of people, the cattle and observing intently the ways of nature was inspiring and a source of delight for Nanadalal. His smaller sketches are testimony of Nandalal's keenness to observe and his empathy for the environment in which he lived. In the present sketch the artist has made a note of the physical form of three women and the folds of their drapery along with an animal study of a cow. Art historian R. Siva Kumar in the book, 'Rhythms of India: The Art of Nandalal Bose' has described the sketches and drawings of Nandalal as - "Nandalal's drawing take through different landscapes and introduce us to life in different cultures- not cosmetically, but intimately. Done on small cards, these drawings are a visual record of the artist's sensory experiences, and they capture the varying moods and gestures with remarkable ease and economy."

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 47
artworks.description: Nandalal in his lifetime, along with other techniques, also mastered the Sino-Japanese painting traditions. In this painting of a female figure, he amalgamates this style with that of the fifth century murals of Ajanta. Elements of the classical cave art can be distinctly seen in the fluid facial features and the gesture of the hands, while the influence of Japanese painting is apparent in the smooth blending of colours and the absence of strong outlines, along with the distinct swirls of the hair.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda(2)' in Bengali on the right upper corner of the painting in reverse.

The quick sweeps of solid, fluid black outline defines the contours of the sketch. A wave of an ornamental red flower in the background lends a delicate feel to the small drawing. Nandalal observed the various facets of nature and rendered them in concise forms in his works.

The light and precise use of brush gives fluidity to the entire painting. The tonal variation of the black colour differentiates between the shadowed and sunlit areas of the spontaneous drawing. Nandalal aimed to capture the entity of the form with least possible means.
