artworks.description: This quick and rough sketch of pen and ink portrays a woman carrying a pot on her head walking along a path with bushes. The contours of the figure are defined with minimum use of lines and the bushes in the background are dashes of ink with dry brush, all in an illustrative style. The clean lines and hurried strokes add elegance to the painting.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '4.12.33' in English vertically in the bottom-left corner of the sketch.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 47
artworks.description: This postcard shows a drawing of a reclining Buddha in the background with a monk at work in the foreground. Nandalal renders the subject in fine, flowing lines, delineated in a realistic representation of the two figures. As the inscription suggests, this may have been sketched at a monastery in Burma (formerly known as Rangoon).

metadata.inscription: Dated '27.12.24' and inscribed 'Rengun' in English in the bottom-right corner. There is another inscription in Bengali that can be roughly translated as, "It will cost you 5 paise".

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 47
artworks.description: This painting belongs to a series of monochromatic ink and watercolour paintings inspired by the Sumi-e Japanese technique the artist employed in the last phase of his life. The use of ink with brush strokes, dark and light, build up tonal variations in this painting of coconut palms. The background has been left bare to focus on the magnificent trees.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali on the bottom-left corner. There is also another inscription in Bengali that can be roughly translated as, 'this, I like' on the bottom-right corner.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 47
artworks.description: Nandalal learnt the technique of leaving white negative space around the subject in the painting from East Asian painting traditions. In this representation of a herd of load-bearing donkeys, the idea is to capture the spirit and not simply reproduce the subject. The range of Nandalal's artistic expression is seen in the changing Indian landscapes, his varied images of nature and the portrayal of people and places.

metadata.inscription: Inscribed 'N.L.Bose, care of D.N.Tagore, Kalingpong, May 1928' in English.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 47
artworks.description: Nandalal had a strong urge to explore new places and people, of which he kept a record in his sketch books. This sketch shows a group of Burmese musicians with a Pwe dancer in the left corner, seen partially. Nandalal carefully depicts the scene of the performance in swift, calligraphic strokes, defining the contours of the figures, adding rhythm and life to the sketch.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '28' and '26.10.24', along the right margin of the sketch. There is an inscription in Bengali that reads, 'village dance' and an inscription in English 'evening?'.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 47
artworks.description: Nandalal understood the significance of the use of lines and experimented frequently in their execution. In this postcard he has rendered a landscape drawing of mountain ranges with their respective names at the peak, in close vicinity, drawn with fine and fluid handling of the line, resulting in a realistic representation of mountains. He did such drawings to hone his understanding of nature in his practice of art.

metadata.inscription: The sketch bears an inscription in English which reads, 'N' (referring to The North location) in the top-left corner of the sketch. There is also another inscription written in Bengali that can be translated as, 'North, South, East and West'.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 47
artworks.description: Nandalal, impressed by the spontaneity of Chinese wash paintings, inculcated the style in his own artistic vocabulary. This monochrome watercolour painting shows thickly forested mountain peaks under a blanket of mist. The trees on the mountains are suggested with brush swabs rather than defined, lending an impressionistic touch.

metadata.inscription: The painting bears the artist's personal seal in the bottom-right corner.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 47
artworks.description: This painting belongs to a series of monochromatic ink and watercolour paintings the artist executed in the last phase of his life. In this painting, the background has been left bare to focus on the magnificent palm trees and birds. The subject is suggested with brush swabs rather than defined strokes, giving an impressionistic touch.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 47
artworks.description: This monochrome landscape painting portrays a snow covered mountain range achieved through varying tones of black colour throughout the postcard. The impressionistic approach of using few lines and tones to create a form, lends a liveliness to the image. Nandalal has used Chinese brush techniques, a soft and flexible flow of the brush in this painting, creating a beautiful landscape.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '3.6.27' in English in the bottom-right corner. The painting also bears the artist's personal seal.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 47
artworks.description: Nandalal portrays in this monochrome watercolour painting, a man asking for alms, wrapped under a thick blanket. The easy and bold use of the brush depicts the male figure with few strokes. The distressed emotion on the man's face is clearly visible even under the thick dabs of colour. The tonal variation of the colour portrays the play of chiaroscuro over the heavily draped figure.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali on the bottom right corner. There is also another inscription, 'Dumka' in Bengali. Dumka is one of the oldest districts of Jharkhand state under Santhal Pargana.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 47
artworks.description: Nandalal throughout his life created thousands of drawings using different linear styles.This sketch probably depicts a scene from a mythological story. The line drawing presents an amalgamation of calligraphic and linear strokes webbed together harmoniously. Thick lines have been used to define the contours of the two male figures, accentuating the underlying pensive emotion of the moment.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '20.5.38' in English on the top left corner. The sketch also bears the artist's personal seal in red.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 47
artworks.description: This watercolour painting of a sunrise has been executed by Nandalal in swift swabs of black colour to represent the trees and birds along with a fiery red to highlight the rising sun in all its glory. The bareness of the sky is complimented by the fullness of the trees in the foreground and the luminescence of the partly visible sun.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali in the top-right corner of the painting.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 47
artworks.description: Nandalal's drawings of places revolve around different motifs and perceptions. This postcard shows a pencil sketch of an evening at Varanasi Ghats with steps leading to the sacred river Ganges, set between the peaceful expanse of sky and water. The wiry use of lines defines the hustle bustle in the atmosphere around the Ghats.

metadata.inscription: The sketch bears an inscription in Bengali that can be translated as, 'Somvar' (referring to day of the week), along the lower margin of the sketch.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 47
artworks.description: In this postcard sketch, Nandalal has depicted a group of people sitting under a hut probably they are making illustration as per the inscriptions, executed in fluid watercolour strokes with dabs and dashes which bring out the forms at their most basic and adding life to the composition.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is an inscription in a form of an informative letter in Bengali which can be translated as, 'We have organized ourselves and started working. The work which is assigned by you would be starting soon. They are presently making the illustrations of the poems from Geetanjali. Accept my regards, Nanda' along the top margin.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 47
artworks.description: Nandalal Bose was indefatigable in his sketching routines which formed an adjunct part of his daily life. From monumental landscapes to the tiniest insect provided subject matter for him. This postcard shows a watercolour study of a bird perched atop a thin branch of a tree. He has filled the drawing with quick dabs of colour and detailed the head, legs and feathers with defining outlines.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali at the bottom of the painting.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 47
artworks.description: This watercolour painting shows a Buddhist burial site amidst the trees over a mountain top. Nandalal portrays the tree laden path towards the site with confident swabs and dabs of colour. The background of the painting is a plain wash of translucent watercolours depicting the snow laden mountain peaks beyond, under a bare sky.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali at the bottom left corner of the painting.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 47
artworks.medium: Pen & ink and watercolor on postcard
artworks.description: This drawing is a rendition of a Shiva sculpture in the style seen on the temples of Khajuraho in Madhya Pradesh and at the Konark Sun temple in Odisha. It is a simple sketch of delicate but confident lines defining the contours of the figure and watery brushstrokes, depicting the iconography of Shiva. The purpose of the brown colour is to convey the look of the stone.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 47
artworks.description: Nandalal understood the significance of the use of lines and experimented frequently in their execution. This postcard shows a self portrait of Nandalal, drawn with thick contouring lines and executed in a calligraphic fashion adding vigour and grace to the portrait. The fluid handling of the line and its strong delineation in his works was the influence of Far Eastern art practices.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 47

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 55
artworks.description: This is one of the paintings from Nandalal's visit to Gopalpur, near Puri, on the eastern Indian coast of Orissa. He has rendered fishermen who are struggling with their canoe in the high tides of the sea with his spontaneous brushstrokes. In this depiction of harmony between human and nature, he has used the ink-wash technique learned from Chinese and Japanese art traditions.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '01.11.1947' in English on the left margin of the postcard.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No.50
artworks.description: In this landscape painting, Nandalal has utilised the tonal variations of black ink with water for creating a recognisable effect of mountains and trees. R. Siva Kumar in the book, 'Rhythms of India: The Art of Nandalal Bose' writes of the artist, "In spite of specificities of location, not all of his drawings were done on location...he gave to works done in the studio the same vividness found in his studies done directly from nature."

metadata.inscription: Dated '24.5.45' in English and signed 'Nanda' in Bengali along the left margin of the sketch.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No.50
artworks.description: In this painting, Nandalal has represented the terraced farms of Darjeeling, located in the foothills of the Himalayas in northern Bengal. The dark patches of ink in the painting indicate the areas of heavy vegetation and trees. This is a landscape in the monochrome ink wash technique, which is associated with specific Chinese and Japanese landscape traditions. It also recalls his statement from his book, 'Vision and Creation', ''Landscapes can be painted in the manner of seas, with wavy heaps of stone and earth.''.

metadata.inscription: Dated '15.5.1945' and signed 'Nanda' in Bengali along the left margin of the postcard. There is an inscription in Bengali that can be translated as ' Darjeeling, Shri Nandalal Bose',below the date

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 55
artworks.description: This artwork has been painted on one of Nandalal's trips to Gopalpur, near Puri, on the eastern Indian coast of Orissa. He was inspired by the daily lives of the Nulia tribe. In this painting, his impulsive brush strokes delineate the Nulia fishermen with their distinctive conical caps, working together in harmony with the surf in order to set their canoe afloat.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '31.10.47' in English at the bottom-left corner of the postcard. There is an inscription in Bengali 'Gopalpur' referring to the place it was sketched at.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 55
artworks.description: This is another of the three drawings in this series that was painted on one of Nandalal's trips to Gopalpur, near Puri, on the eastern Indian coast of Orissa. Here he has depicted the local fishermen at work. His spontaneous brush strokes delineate the struggle with their canoes at the seashore during a high tide. Nandalal has made this complete picture with the amalgamation of strength and traditional systems of a tribe.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '31.10.1947' in English at the bottom-left corner of the postcard.

The above watercolour illustration by Nandalal is a representation of a mountainscape executed by harmoniously diluting the tones of the colours with sweeping brush strokes, a technique the artist acquired from the arts of the Far East.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 63
artworks.description: Nandalal is known to have fervently sketched on postcard sized papers mostly using ink and brush, recording his surroundings. His small sketches vastly vary in detailing, some drawn quickly with just a few lines, others executed with more elaborate characteristics from an analytical perspective. His search for newer forms of expression and his inner urge to constantly innovate is well reflected in the multiple postcards in the collection of the museum which portray the artist's visual experiences of flora fauna, the people, their attires, life in rural villages, the landscapes, etc. Dinkar Kowshik in his article 'Drawings and Sketches of Nandalal in the book, "Nandalal Bose - A collection of Essays" has written of Nandalal's sketches and drawings - "Much of his (Nandalal) strength and sensitive wealth finds expression in the spontaneity of his sketches. They are a veritable treasure of shrewd observation, powerful calligraphy, psychological insight, rich sallies of humour and emphatic portrayal of the flora and fauna." This particular sketch illustrates a woman leisurely seated on the floor with a cloth bag and a pair of weighing dishes.

artworks.description: Nandalal had a strong affinity for sketching, his subjects being the surrounding environs, people in their everyday life or anything that he found fascinating. The fluid handling of the lines and their strong delineation in the calligraphic style gives a textured rendition to the body of the local carrying an infant on his shoulders and a bamboo stick in his left hand and also accentuates his vigour and strength. Dinkar Kowshik in his article 'Drawings and Sketches of Nandalal in the book, "Nandalal Bose - A collection of Essays" has elucidated about the sketches of Nandalal in the words, "Nandalal's drawings are vast in number and varied in technical interest. He was indefatigable in his search for form and to the end of his life he remained a student. Whatever he saw, and wherever he went he recorded the flora and fauna, the people of the place, their dress, their carriages, the head-dresses, the landscape, the festivals, the architecture, and while doing that he went on attaining a felicity of expression. His drawings often on card size format turned into independent works of art; they were fresh and vivid because of their immediacy and rapport with felt reality. They were not preliminary sketches to be developed later into painting. In fact most of these drawings and sketches were an end in themselves. Their compositional relation to the blank space, their shrewd sense of observation, and their living organic quality make his sketches an end in themselves. Their compositional relation to the blank space, their shrewd sense of observation, and their living organic quality make his sketches far more absorbing aesthetically than many of his finished paintings."

artworks.description: Nandalal Bose, adept in the Chinese and Japanese brush techniques has in this monochromatic painting emphasised on the tonal variations of the distinctive form of a traveller on a mountain pony in the foreground. As inscribed by the artist himself, Nandalal executed this hilly landscape from his memory, depicting his probable sojourn to Rajgriha hills (now Rajgir hills, a Buddhist pilgrimage site in the Indian state of Bihar. Art historian, R. Siva Kumar in the book, 'Rhythms of India: The Art of Nandalal Bose' writes, "In spite of specificities of location, not all of his drawings were done on location. Nandalal used drawing as a part of his pedagogic method, as a technique to awaken students' impulses to explore experiential realities, but at the same time he insisted that they do both, studies from nature and drawings from memory.....Much like Chinese and Japanese painters (and Rembrandt, for that matter), he gave to works done in the studio the same vividness found in his studies done directly from nature." artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 64
artworks.description: Nandalal Bose also mastered the Sino- Japanese techniques of painting being first influenced by Okakura Kakuzo and the train of Japanese artists who visited India after him especially Arai Kampo. The blurring of the linear outlines of figures and the harmonious dilution of colours were techniques Nandalal acquired from the arts of the Far East. In the above painting, Nandalal uses a series of diverse tones and brush strokes to illustrate a rocky, trodden mountain path from his memory. A figure of a human standing on the cliff is suggested with a small blot of colour. The adept use of the inherent white space and slight shade differences in the intensity of a single black colour showcases Nandalal's prowess in the art of monochromatic painting.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 64
artworks.description: Nandalal Bose explored a wide range of traditions to arrive at his unique visual language and has left behind a large corpus of works in a wide variety of styles, expressions and techniques. In the above monochromatic painting, Nandalal executes a hilly landscape from his memory using Far Eastern techniques of modulating tones and blurring outlines.

Regarding the sea drawings, Nandalal in his book, 'Vision and Creation' writes, "The Sea offers an endless, ever-moving image. At times, it looks like the thousand-hooded Anantanaga (primordial serpent), as it rears and hisses and then runs away; or like the unharnessed and wild horses of the sea-god, it seems to be prancing around. On the crest of the breaking waves one can get a glimpse of tongues of fire or the claws of a dragon. To catch this in a picture is, in a sense, attempting the impossible."

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 66
artworks.description: Nandalal Bose had a strong affinity for sketching, his subjects being the surrounding environs, people in their everyday life, animals or anything that he found fascinating. In the above painting, the fluid brushwork and its strong delineation in the calligraphic style adds vigour, movement and life to the human figures. The waves of the sea are executed in bold sweeping strokes. Nandalal Bose in his book, 'On Art' writes- "To acquire right knowledge and perception one should study men and animals when they are on the move or are active: when one can note in action the how and wherefore of the body's muscles, tendons and joints. Such study makes for useful knowledge and its easy retention in mind. Such knowledge, without doubt, is natural and living."

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 67
artworks.description: In this drawing, Nandalal has illustrated the waves of the sea along the coast of Puri. He has depicted the waves in curvilinear strokes of the pen while straight, swift strokes depict the infinite sky. Regarding the sea drawings, in his book, 'Vision and Creation' he writes, "The sea offers an endless, ever-moving image. At times, it looks like the thousand-hooded Anantanag (primordial serpent), as it rears and hisses and then runs away; or like the unharnessed and wild horses of the sea-god, it seems to be prancing around. On the crest of the breaking waves one can get a glimpse of tongues of fire or the claws of a dragon. To catch this in a picture is, in a sense, attempting the impossible."

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 70
artworks.description: Nandalal had a strong affinity for sketching, his subjects being the surrounding environs, people in their everyday life or anything that he found fascinating. Nandalal in the above pen and ink sketch has portrayed a man and two children, sitting around a small fire against the backdrop of thatched huts, using varying linear strokes of the stylus. The suggestion of the smoke searing up from the bonfire is also made through linear streaks rising up in the air. Nandalal had firm belief that for the creation of art an intimate understanding of the nature and its ways is imperative. His smaller sketches are testimony of Nandalal's keenness to observe and his empathy for the environment in which he lived. Jaya Appaswamy in her article, 'Nandalal Bose- Master Draughtsman' writes- "The drawings on postcards have a spontaneity and brevity not seen in more formal works. They exist as evidence of the artist's unceasing desire to master visual data."

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 70
artworks.description: Nandalal was indefatigable in his sketching routines which formed an adjunct part of his daily life. Making instantaneous visual records of anything amusing happening in his surroundings or of social events, or observing the demeanour and mannerisms of people, the cattle and observing intently the ways of nature was inspiring and a source of delight for Nanadalal. His smaller sketches are testimony of Nandalal's keenness to observe and his empathy for the environment in which he lived. In this sketch the artist has faithfully represented the anatomy and the predatory instincts of the large cat with the spontaneity of the brushwork. The fluid handling of the line and their strong delineation was the influence of the Far Eastern art practices. Nandalal understood the significance of the use of lines and experimented frequently in their execution from fine lines to being thick contouring lines and executed in a calligraphic fashion. Art historian R. Siva Kumar in the book, 'Rhythms of India: The Art of Nandalal Bose' has described the sketches and drawings of Nandalal as - "Nandalal's drawing take through different landscapes and introduce us to life in different cultures- not cosmetically, but intimately. Done on small cards, these drawings are a visual record of the artist's sensory experiences, and they capture the varying moods and gestures with remarkable ease and economy."

artworks.description: Nandalal adept in the Chinese and Japanese brush techniques has in this monochromatic painting portrayed a woman labourer carrying mortar and bricks on her head for construction of a wall. The representation of the woman with fluid lines in the far Eastern calligraphic style artist has been executed in a minimalist fashion. Nandalal was indefatigable in his sketching routines which formed an adjunct part of his daily life. Making instantaneous visual records of anything amusing happening in his surroundings or of social events, or observing the demeanour and mannerisms of people, the cattle and observing intently the ways of nature was inspiring and a source of delight for Nanadalal. His smaller sketches are testimony of Nandalal's keenness to observe and his empathy for the environment in which he lived. Art historian R. Siva Kumar in the book, 'Rhythms of India: The Art of Nandalal Bose' has described the sketches and drawings of Nandalal as - "Nandalal's drawing take through different landscapes and introduce us to life in different cultures- not cosmetically, but intimately. Done on small cards, these drawings are a visual record of the artist's sensory experiences, and they capture the varying moods and gestures with remarkable ease and economy."

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 72
artworks.description: Dinkar Kowshik in his article 'Drawings and Sketches of Nandalal' in the book, "Nandalal Bose - A collection of Essays" writes, "Much of his (Nandalal) strength and sensitive wealth finds expression in the spontaneity of his sketches. They are a veritable treasure of shrewd observation, powerful calligraphy, psychological insight, rich sallies of humour and emphatic portrayal of the flora and fauna." National Gallery of Modern Art, New Delhi acquired the largest collection of 6744 artworks of Nandalal Bose from his family, some of which were exhibited in the Centenary celebratory exhibition organised by the museum in 1983. A major portion of the museum's collection includes monochromatic pencil sketches, pen and ink drawings on postcard and paper, watercolour paintings and sketches apart from the more detailed and elaborate tempera and wash paintings, Haripura posters and prints from the artist's extensive oeuvre.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 72, 1925
artworks.description: National Gallery of Modern Art, New Delhi acquired the largest collection of 6744 artworks of Nandalal Bose from his family, some of which were exhibited in the Centenary celebratory exhibition organised by the museum in 1983. A major portion of the museum's collection includes monochromatic pencil sketches, pen and ink drawings on postcard and paper, watercolour paintings and sketches apart from the more detailed and elaborate tempera and wash paintings, Haripura posters and prints from the artist's extensive oeuvre. Nandalal preferred drawing from life, often sketching outdoors with the subject being life, nature studies, landscapes, figure drawings, animals. Often the sketches were small in scale although invigorating with the rich detailing of the artist's observations, experiences and sojourns to various places.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 72
artworks.description: The fluid handling of the line and their strong delineation in the calligraphic style adds grace and spirit to the subjecst narrated in the drawings and sketches of Nandalal Bose. The folds of the drapes, their coiffures, ornaments and their implements are keenly observed by the artist. In the present sketch three men wearing the traditional Indian Dhoti, turban and carrying swords in thier hands are either engaged in a contest or are practicing their martial arts. artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 79
artworks.medium: Pen and ink and pencil on postcard
artworks.description: Nandalal preferred drawing from life, often sketching outdoors with the subject being life, nature studies, landscapes, figure drawings, animals. Often the sketches were small in scale although invigorating with the rich detailing of the artist's observations, experiences and sojourns to various places. In this pen and ink drawing the artist has portrayed a man carrying a pile of hay across his shoulders walking with the aid of a stick. Noted art historian Dinkar Kowshik in his article 'Drawings and Sketches of Nandalal in the book, "Nandalal Bose - A collection of Essays" has elucidated about the sketches of Nandalal in the words, "Nandalal's sketches in fact provide a moving record of a humble life and natural environment in which he lived. These are not in any way preliminary studies for his larger finished compositions in black and white or in colour. They are finished and self-contained in themselves like a Japanese 'Haiku'. Their spacing, their distribution of black and white, their linear or tonal accents and the signature all form a part of a single unit."

metadata.inscription: Signed and dated 'Nanda 15.11.53' in Bengali along the right margin of the painting with pen and black ink. The painting also bears an inscription in Bengali which can be translated as 'Towards the end'.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 79
artworks.medium: Pen and ink and pencil on postcard
artworks.description: In this sketch the artist has represented a woman seated on a round cane stool with her purse and slippers lying next to her on the ground. The fluid handling of the line and their strong delineation in the calligraphic style adds grace and spirit to the form of the woman. The artist has astutely noted the finer details of the subject as the folds of her drapes, her long plaited hair, and the cheerful expressions. The lively sense of humour arising from these humble records of the everyday chores of common folks is testimony of Nandalal's keen sense of observation and his empathy for the environment in which he lived.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 79
artworks.medium: Pen and ink and pencil on postcard
artworks.description: Nandalal had a strong affinity for sketching; his subjects being from the surrounding environs, people in their everyday life or anything that he found fascinating. He had firm belief that for the creation of art an intimate understanding of the nature and its ways is imperative. The range of Nandalal's artistic expression can be seen in the changing Indian landscapes, his varied images of nature and the portrayal of people and places. Dinkar Kowshik in his article 'Drawings and Sketches of Nandalal in the book, "Nandalal Bose - A collection of Essays" has written of Nandalal's sketches and drawings - "Much of his (Nandalal) strength and sensitive wealth finds expression in the spontaneity of his sketches. They are a veritable treasure of shrewd observation, powerful calligraphy, psychological insight, rich sallies of humour and emphatic portrayal of the flora and fauna." In this particular sketch the artist has portrayed a fisherman, seated with his fish displayed in front of him probably for selling. The artist has with the fluid handling of the line and its strong delineation in the calligraphic style lent grace and spirit to the form of the figure. The folds of the drapes, coiffure, ornaments and the weighing implement have been keenly observed by the artist in the sketch.

He had firm belief that for the creation of art an intimate understanding of the nature and its ways is imperative. The range of Nandalal's artistic expression can be seen in the changing Indian landscapes, his varied images of nature and the portrayal of people and places. Dinkar Kowshik in his article 'Drawings and Sketches of Nandalal in the book, "Nandalal Bose - A collection of Essays" has written of Nandalal's sketches and drawings - "Much of his (Nandalal) strength and sensitive wealth finds expression in the spontaneity of his sketches. They are a veritable treasure of shrewd observation, powerful calligraphy, psychological insight, rich sallies of humour and emphatic portrayal of the flora and fauna." In this particular sketch the artist has portrayed three villagers passing through the fields with one of them carrying canned buckets tied across the stick and held onto the shoulder while the other is shown as carrying a canned basket atop his ahead. The artist has with the fluid handling of the line and its strong delineation in the calligraphic style lent grace and spirit to the form of the figures. The folds of their drapes, their coiffures, ornaments and their implements have been keenly observed by the artist in the sketch.

The artist in this pen and ink drawing has represented an old man playing cymbals, a musical instrument often used by wandering minstrels who preach religious scriptures and divinity through music and folk songs. Nandalal has in his individualistic style emphasized on the line drawings with their solidity of structure for rendering the drawing of the bearded man. The fluid handling of the line and their strong delineation was the influence of the Far Eastern art practices. artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 81
artworks.description: Nandalal had a strong affinity for sketching, his subjects being the surrounding environs, people in their everyday life or anything that he found fascinating. His firm belief that for the creation of art an intimate understanding of the nature and its ways is imperative. The range of Nandalal's artistic expression can be seen in the changing Indian landscapes, his varied images of nature and the portrayal of people and places.Dinkar Kowshik in his article 'Drawings and Sketches of Nandalal in the book, "Nandalal Bose - A collection of Essays" has written of Nandalal's sketches and drawings - "Much of his (Nandalal) strength and sensitive wealth finds expression in the spontaneity of his sketches. They are a veritable treasure of shrewd observation, powerful calligraphy, psychological insight, rich sallies of humour and emphatic portrayal of the flora and fauna." In this particular sketch the fluid handling of the line and their strong delineation in the calligraphic style adds grace and spirit to the group of a village farmers carrying their implements.The folds of the drapes, their coiffures, ornaments and their implements have been keenly observed by the artist in the sketch.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 81
artworks.description: Nandalal had a strong affinity for sketching, his subjects being the surrounding environs, people in their everyday life or anything that he found fascinating. In this pen and ink drawing can be seen a man carrying his belongings in cane baskets tied to a bamboo bar across the fields. Nandalal in his individualistic style has emphasized on the line with their solidity of structure. The calligraphic line drawing brings out the rhythm and coherence in the form of his subjects rather than imitation in formal resemblance. Dinkar Kowshik in his article 'Drawings and Sketches of Nandalal in the book, "Nandalal Bose - A collection of Essays" has elucidated about the sketches of Nandalal in the words,"Nandalal's drawings are vast in number and varied in technical interest. He was indefatigable in his search for form and to the end of his life he remained a student. Whatever he saw, and wherever he went he recorded the flora and fauna, the people of the place, their dress, their carriages, the head-dresses, the landscape, the festivals, the architecture, and while doing that he went on attaining a felicity of expression. His drawings often on card size format turned into independent works of art; they were fresh and vivid because of their immediacy and rapport with felt reality. They were not preliminary sketches to be developed later into painting. In fact most of these drawings and sketches were an end in themselves. Their compositional relation to the blank space, their shrewd sense of observation, and their living organic quality make his sketches an end in themselves. Their compositional relation to the blank space, their shrewd sense of observation, and their living organic quality make his sketches far more absorbing aesthetically than many of his finished paintings."

But in spite of all such variations, all human figures are united in general structure, in forms and function of muscles and tendons, in shapes and characters of their various limbs."

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 83
artworks.description: Nandalal had a strong affinity for sketching, his subjects being the surrounding environs, people in their everyday life or anything that he found fascinating. The fluid handling of the lines and their strong delineation in the calligraphic style gives a textured rendition to the body of the local carrying baskets across his shoulders and also accentuates his vigour and strength. Dinkar Kowshik in his article 'Drawings and Sketches of Nandalal in the book, "Nandalal Bose - A collection of Essays" has elucidated about the sketches of Nandalal in the words,"Nandalal's drawings are vast in number and varied in technical interest. He was indefatigable in his search for form and to the end of his life he remained a student. Whatever he saw, and wherever he went he recorded the flora and fauna, the people of the place, their dress, their carriages, the head-dresses, the landscape, the festivals, the architecture, and while doing that he went on attaining a felicity of expression. His drawings often on card size format turned into independent works of art; they were fresh and vivid because of their immediacy and rapport with felt reality. They were not preliminary sketches to be developed later into painting. In fact most of these drawings and sketches were an end in themselves. Their compositional relation to the blank space, their shrewd sense of observation, and their living organic quality make his sketches an end in themselves. Their compositional relation to the blank space, their shrewd sense of observation, and their living organic quality make his sketches far more absorbing aesthetically than many of his finished paintings."

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 84
artworks.description: Nandalal is known to have fervently sketched on postcard sized papers mostly using ink and brush, recording his surroundings. His small sketches vastly vary in detailing, some drawn quickly with just a few lines, others executed with more elaborate characteristics from an analytical perspective. His search for newer forms of expression is well reflected in the multiple postcards in the collection of the museum which portray his visual experiences of mostly nature and rural life and also of his inner urge to constantly innovate. In this pen and ink drawing an old woman is depicted sitting in front of her thatched hut and making fire with utensils and earthen pots lying close to her. A small canoe can also be seen inside the hut. Nandalal has in his individualistic style emphasized on the line drawings with their solidity of structure. The calligraphic line drawing brings out the rhythm and coherence in the form of his subjects rather than imitation in formal resemblance. A. Ramachandran in the book, 'Rhythms of India: The Art of Nandalal Bose' writes, "He made quick graphic impressions, often simplifying them to just few lines as he sought to understand the inherent structure of what he was seeing. At times he recorded objects in a more analytical way, while at others he transformed them into visual codes of pattern."

His intent being to understand and assimilate the various artistic elements involved for excelling in his domain and which also enriched his own visual vocabulary. The fluid handling of the brush and the strong delineation of the fine and bold contouring lines not only lends tonal variations but also assists in true representation of the tree and birds as well.

Nandalal Bose in his book 'Vision and Creation' writes, "A tree grows upward; it is driven by a singular urge to spread towards the sky- trunk, branch and leaf. The trunk is like the tree's backbone; so its characteristic rhythm has to be drawn first; then its main structure with branch and twig; and finally, the total image with its bunches of leaves and shoots..."

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 86
artworks.description: Nandalal had a strong affinity for sketching; his subjects being from the surrounding environs, people in their everyday life or anything that he found fascinating. The artist has executed this humorous sketch of a feline keenly observing the single leaf in black as it sways with the wind. The inscription at the bottom of the painting in Bengali described the drawing as such. Nandalal has used delicate lines to create the form of the feline, the tree, the leaves and the environ in the backdrop. The artist emphasised on the strong delineation of line in the calligraphic style in his works which was the influence of the Far Eastern art practices. Nandalal developed his unique visual language using fine lines to thick contouring lines for rendering his subjects and to bring about the tonal variations using simple strokes to bring about the corporeality of form and substance. Dinkar Kowshik in his article 'Drawings and Sketches of Nandalal in the book titled "Nandalal Bose - A collection of Essays" has elucidated about the sketches of Nandalal in the words, "Nandalal's sketches in fact provide a moving record of a humble life and natural environment in which he lived. These are not in any way preliminary studies for his larger finished compositions in black and white or in colour. They are finished and self-contained in themselves like a Japanese 'Haiku'. Their spacing, their distribution of black and white, their linear or tonal accents and the signature all form a part of a single unit."

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 86
artworks.description: Nandalal adept in the Chinese and Japanese brush techniques has in this monochromatic painting recorded a celebratory scene of a gala organised in Santiniketan with students relaxing, the benches and desk lying disarranged suggesting of the merriment on the campus. The utilisation of tonal variations of the black colour for recognisable renderation of the assembly of students underneath the thatched roofed buildings of the institution and against the backdrop of tall woods is intriguing and alluring at the same time. Nandalal was indefatigable in his sketching routines which formed an adjunct part of his daily life. Making instantaneous visual records of anything amusing happening in his surroundings or of social events, or observing the demeanour and mannerisms of people, the cattle and observing intently the ways of nature was inspiring and a source of delight for Nanadalal. His smaller sketches are testimony of Nandalal's keenness to observe and his empathy for the environment in which he lived.

artworks.description: In this delightful pen and ink drawing, Nandalal has portrayed a woman nursing her young one sitting underneath a tree. The fluid handling of the line and their strong delineation in the calligraphic style adds grace and spirit to the subject. The folds of the drapes of the woman, her coiffure, ornaments and the stance of her body are keenly observed by the artist. The perceptible representation of both the tree and the woman is executed in a range of linear styles with pen and ink that not only lends tonal variations but brings out their true form as well. The artist has astutely dealt with the spatial treatment of the woman sitting against the tree and employed the use of linear patterns to bring out the form of the branches and the leaves of the tree. The drawing also encapsulates the compassion and warmth of the scene.

Eminent artist A. Ramachandran in the book, 'Rhythms of India: The Art of Nandalal Bose' has made the following observation about Nandalal's drawings and sketches - "He made quick graphic impressions, often simplifying them to just few lines as he sought to understand the inherent structure of what he was seeing. In this delightful pen and ink drawing, Nandalal has portrayed a mother affectionately holding her child's hand and is tending to her gently.The perceptible representation of both the mother and the young one is executed by the use of delicate yet free flowing lines with pen and ink that also lends to the tonal variations to their form and drapes. The perceptible representation is executed with a range of linear styles with pen and ink that lends tonal variations and brings out the true form of the repairman or carpenter. The trunk of the contoured tree is wittily illustrated to take the shape of a man's facial features. The presence of a thatched roof in the backdrop and the group of hens affirms of the rural setting of the sketch.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 89
artworks.description: Nandalal's exploration of the different ways of delineating a line allowed him to experiment in representation of lines in its varying forms adding rhythm, vigour and life to the forms of nature. In the above hilly landscape, the perceptible representation of the pine trees with their ridged surfaces is executed with a range of strokes that lends tonal variations, texture and brings out the true form of the trees. The adept use of the inherent white space in the foreground and water-body with scribbled strokes showcases Nandalal's prowess as a draftsman.

metadata.inscription: The painting has an inscription which reads, 'Paila Baisakh, 1364, Santiniketan, Nandalal Bose' in Bengali at the left bottom corner of the painting with pen and ink. 'Paila Baisakh 1364' means the first month of the Bengali year 1364.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 89
artworks.description: Nandalal Bose is known to have fervently sketched on postcard sized papers mostly using ink and brush, recording his surroundings. His small sketches vastly vary in detailing, some drawn quickly with just a few lines, others executed with more elaborate characteristics from an analytical perspective. In the above painting, Nandalal employs brush and black colour to study the form and texture of the ornamental flowers- 'Hibiscus' and 'Kadamba'. The artist's use of fluid handling of the line and their strong delineation was the influence of the Far Eastern art practices. Nandalal Bose in his book, 'On Art' says, "Nature is life itself and teeming always with infinite variety; it is in her that the artist always renews his experience and finds an unceasing flow of inspiration."

metadata.inscription: Signed and dated 'Nanda, 7.57' in Bengali along the right margin of the painting with brush and black colour.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 89
artworks.description: Nandalal Bose's drawings, complete in themselves, were his vivid observations of the characteristics and attributes of subjects chosen from his immediate surroundings. In this particular postcard, Nandalal illustrates a man sitting atop a wooden purlin, occupied in making a thatched roof, supported by several sections of bamboo canes. The fluid handling of the line and its graphic quality adds vigour and life to the form of the working man. Jaya Appaswamy in her article, 'Nandalal Bose- Master Draughtsman' writes- "The drawings on postcards have a spontaneity and brevity not seen in more formal works. They exist as evidence of the artist's unceasing desire to master visual data."

metadata.inscription: Signed and dated 'Nanda, 27.3.57' in Bengali at the bottom centre of the painting with pen and black ink.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 89
artworks.description: Nandalal created a visual language by the use of simple lines, tones and strokes to model and bring about a corporeality of form and substance. In the above postcard, Nandalal illustrates a woman glancing out from a window. Nandalal uses delicate lines that create the visual effect of a sari, clinging to the woman's body. The series of slanting strokes also suggest rainfall. The range of Nandalal's artistic expression can be seen in his varied images of nature and the portrayal of people and places.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 89
artworks.medium: Pen and ink and pencil on postcard
artworks.description: Nandalal Bose was indefatigable in his sketching routines which formed an adjunct part of his daily life. Making instantaneous visual records of anything amusing happening in his surroundings or of social events, or observing the demeanour and mannerisms of people cattle and observing intently the ways of nature was inspiring and a source of delight for Nandalal. His smaller sketches are testimony of Nandalal's keenness to observe and his empathy for the environment in which he lived. Dinkar Kowshik in his book, 'Nandalal Bose: The Doyen of Indian Art', writes- "Drawing was a definition, a distillation of form. Through line, several individual variations of form were brought together, condensed, simplified and expressed in a general, universal statement." This particular drawing illustrates a woman who is probably grinding spices on a traditional ground stone.

In the above sketch the artist has depicted women dancing amidst trees and celebrating an Indian festival Holi which is celebrated during Dol Purnima (full moon day) as suggested in the inscription. The dancing figures, the trees and the falling leaves in the composition are rendered with thick, bold ink strokes. The lines are fluid yet firm invigorating vigour and dynamism in the composition.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' and dated '1359 (referring to the Bengali Year) in Bengali along the lower margin of the postcard with black ink. There is an inscription in Bengali that can be translated as 'Dol Purnima' along the lower margin of the postcard with black ink.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Album No. 92
artworks.medium: Pen and ink and pencil on postcard
artworks.description: This postcard shows a rendition of two dimensional stylised leaves on a rectangular relief panel, part of a longer panel around the Peepal tree as the inscription suggest .Nandalal has darkened the recesses between two leaves with a linear pattern to convey the depth of the carving. The sketch portrays Nandalal's impulse to imitate the motif in its original form to enrich his knowledge of design and ornamental work.

metadata.inscription: The sketch bears an inscription in Bengali that can be translated as, 'a motif panel near a Peepal tree, in Puri' along the lower margin of the postcard.

artworks.title: Sketch from Drawing Book No. 3
artworks.description: Nandalal preferred drawing from life, often sketching outdoors with the subject being life, nature studies, landscapes, figure drawings and animals. Often the sketches were small in scale although invigorating with the rich detailing of the artist's observations. This sketch by Nandalal is one such study of a Dragon Fly. Besides a detailed drawing of the insect, he has also scribbled notes about its anatomy, such as structure and colour.

metadata.inscription: There are inscriptions in Bengali that detail the insect's structure, colours and anatomical details. There is another inscription in English that reads, 'Dragon Fly'.

artworks.title: Sketch from Drawing Book No. 4
artworks.description: Nandalal had a strong affinity for sketching, his subjects being the surrounding environs, people in their everyday life or anything that he found fascinating. In the sketch above, he has divided a postcard into three sections and made three sketches on it. Each sketch is the magnified rendition of its left-adjacent sketch. artworks.title: Sketch from Drawing Book No. 4

artworks.title: Sketch from Drawing Book No. 9
artworks.medium: Pen ink and pencil on paper
artworks.description: Nandalal had a firm belief that for the creation of art an intimate understanding of nature and its way is imperative. He made instantaneous visual records of anything amusing happening in his surroundings, the subjects being life, nature studies, landscapes, figure drawings, animals. In this postcard, Nandalal has made two drawing of the same fish from different profiles. The detailed pencil drawings have been reproduced later with pen. The fluid handling of the lines defines the contours while the short strokes suggest the modelling of the form, resulting in the realistic representation of the fish.

metadata.inscription: There are two inscriptions in Bengali that read 'Jonon indrio' (reproductive organ)below the drawing horizontally and 'Patar moto'(leaf like structure) below the drawing vertically.

artworks.title: Sketch from Drawing Book No. 16
artworks.description: Nandalal preferred drawing from life, often sketching outdoors with the subject being life, nature studies, landscapes, figure drawings, animals and birds or anything that he found fascinating. In his pencil sketches he has experimented with the use of lines to attain texture, vigour and life to the form of the figure. This particular sketch illustrates a woman doing up her hair. Her curvaceous body and the drapes of her saree are manifested through fluid handling of lines which adds grace and sensuality to the subject. The sublime expression of the woman is particularly well represented.

artworks.title: Sketch from Drawing Book No. 16
artworks.description: Nandalal in his pencil sketches has experimented with lines to attain texture, to add vigour and life to the form of the figure. The sketch portrays an expressive form and graceful movement of the female dancer. The uniformly bold lines suggest the modelling of the body and facial features, adding grace to the feminine form. Nandalal has made a clear observation of the lyricism in the dance movement and the devotion with which it is performed. The sublime expressions of the woman and the folds of her sari are particularly well represented.

artworks.title: Sketch from Drawing Book No. 16

The strokes are quick and smudged, conveying the movement of the bird.

artworks.title: Sketch from Drawing Book No. 16
artworks.description: In this delightful drawing the artist has represented three women collecting flowers. The fluid handling of the line and its strong delineation in the calligraphic style suggests the modelling of the body, facial features, adding grace and spirit to the feminine forms. The sublime expressions of the women and the folds of their sarees are particularly well represented. The leaves of the trees in the background are drawn with quick strokes. A. Ramachandran in the book, 'Rhythms of India: The Art of Nandalal Bose ' writes, ''He made quick graphic impressions, often simplifying them to just a few lines as he sought to understand the inherent structure of what he was seeing. At times he recorded objects in a more analytical way, while at others he transformed them into visual codes of pattern.''
