artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 8
artworks.description: This sketch by Nandalal portrays an ornamental representation of a lion. In a style often seen on temple architecture and as decorative objects in the north eastern parts of India, as well as in Nepal and regions of East Asia.

metadata.inscription: Inscribed "Nepali (Darjeeling mal)" vertically along the left margin of the sketch referring to the place it was sketched at.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 8
artworks.description: Nandalal had a strong affinity for sketching, his subjects being the surrounding environs, people in their everyday life or anything that he found fascinating. In this sketch, he renders an earthen or ceramic jug in long, loose strokes of a pencil.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 8
artworks.description: Nandalal had a strong affinity for sketching, his subjects being the surrounding environs, people in their everyday life or anything that he found fascinating. In this sketch he renders an earthen vessel that he encountered on one of his travels to the Ajanta caves in Maharashtra, in long, loose strokes of a pencil.

metadata.inscription: There are two inscriptions in English, 'Ajanta' along the left margin and 'Earthen', along the right margin of the sketch.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 8
artworks.description: In this pencil sketch, Nandalal renders two designs of water-pipes or hookas commonly smoked across South Asia. This is one among many such sketches of hookas from various places that Nandalal has documented in this album, detailing and recording regional variations in its designs.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 8
artworks.description: This is another one of Nandalal's quickly executed sketches. Characterised by their loose strokes and outlines, their purpose is to serve as an exploration of forms at their most basic. Stripping it of superfluous detail, only the bare minimum remains. This particular sketch depicts an earthen pot the artist came across at the Ajanta caves in Ayrangabad, Maharashtra.

metadata.inscription: There are two inscriptions in English that read, 'Earthen' and 'Ajanta', referring to the place it was sketched at, in Maharashtra, India.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 8
artworks.description: In this simple line sketch, Nandalal has rendered two earthen vessels, a pot placed over another. Its spherical contours have been depicted by the artist in a series of concentric circles not taking away from its three-dimensionality.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 8
artworks.description: Nandalal had a strong affinity for sketching, his subjects being the surrounding environs, people in their everyday life or anything that he found fascinating. In this sketch he renders an earthen or ceramic vessel he encountered at the ancient Buddhist site of Sarnath, in long, loose strokes of the brush.

metadata.inscription: Dated '2.1.30' and inscribed 'Sarnath' in Bengali along the lower margin of the sketch.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 8
artworks.description: In this postcard-sized sketch, Nandalal has portrayed the various kinds of pots and vessels he encountered on his travels across the country. These include earthen as well as other materials.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 8
artworks.description: Nandalal has here rendered a floral motif in frottage - the technique of rubbing pencil on paper placed over a textured surface to get an impression of the pattern below. The sketch portrays Nandalal's impulse to imitate the motif in its original form to enrich his knowledge of design and ornamental work.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 8
artworks.description: In this sketch Nandalal has reproduced the design of a carved architectural element, probably a tombstone. The artist often made records of ornamental carvings on historical buildings as he had a deep appreciation for the rich artistic traditions of India and frequently incorporated elements from them in his works.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 8
artworks.description: Nandalal had a strong affinity for sketching, his subjects being the surrounding environs, people in their everyday life or anything that he found fascinating. He has, in this sketch, reproduced the design of an Indian blouse, a women's garment worn in several parts of the subcontinent.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 8
artworks.description: This pencil sketch by Nandalal is the depiction of an architectural bracket with a dragon face carved at its end.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 8
artworks.description: In this sketch, Nandalal has reproduced an architectural bracket, a pillar elegantly carved and a sickle. The artist often made records of ornamental carvings on historical buildings as he had a deep appreciation for the rich artistic traditions of India and frequently incorporated elements from them in his works.

metadata.inscription: There is an inscription in Bengali that can be translated as 'Reversed Sickle, blunt edges' below the image.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 8
artworks.description: In this sketch, Nandalal has reproduced an architectural bracket, elegantly carved in the shape of an elephant's head. The artist often made records of ornamental carvings on historical buildings as he had a deep appreciation for the rich artistic traditions of India and frequently incorporated elements from them in his works.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 8
artworks.description: In this quick pencil sketch, Nandalal has portrayed snapshots of a man's footwear, his finger with a ring and his face in profile. These postcard sketches by the artist were swift visual records of anything that fascinated him in his environment and enriched his creative lexicon.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Sketch Book No.8
artworks.description: Nandalal preferred drawing from life, often sketching outdoors with the subject being life, nature studies, landscapes, figure drawings and animals. In this sketch, he has rendered a sculptural representation of a duck toy, with fluid, smudge strokes of colour pencil delineating the form.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 8
artworks.description: Nandalal has, in this sketch, reproduced several templates of ornamental designs of earrings from the region of Gujarat. He had a deep appreciation for indigenous designs and motifs and often made visual records of these, wherever he encountered them.

metadata.inscription: There are two inscriptions in Bengali that can be translated as, "Gujarati ear ornaments" and "the flower of the Bel plant".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 8
artworks.description: This is another one of Nandalal's quickly executed sketches. Characterised by their loose strokes and outlines, their purpose is to serve as an exploration of forms at their most basic. Stripping it of superfluous detail, only the bare minimum remains. This particular sketch depicts several earthen and metallic pots the artist came across on his travels.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 8
artworks.description: Nandalal has, in this sketch, reproduced several templates of ornamental designs of earrings. He had a deep appreciation for indigenous designs and motifs and often made visual records of these, wherever he encountered them.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 8
artworks.description: In this line drawing, Nandalal has studied the ikat pattern on a blanket and specified its colour scheme in detail. Ikat is a weaving technique popular in India, Indonesia and Japan.

metadata.inscription: Inscribed 'Kambol' in Bengali which can be translated as 'Blanket' in English. There are other inscriptions in Bengali specifying colours such as White, Black, Blue and Orange.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 8
artworks.description: In this quick pencil sketch Nandalal has explored the form of a man, his posture, profile and footwear. Noting carefully the folds of his clothes, the details of his slipper and the contours of his face, the artist renders them in parts on a single postcard.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 8
artworks.description: Nandalal is known to have fervently sketched on postcard sized papers recording his surroundings. His small sketches vastly vary in detailing, some drawn quickly with just a few lines, others executed with more elaborate characteristics from an analytical perspective. In the sketch above, he has depicted an earthen vessel from Birbhum near Santiniketan.

metadata.inscription: There is an inscription in Bengali that can be translated as, "An earthen vessel from Birbhum".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: Nandalal renders an aged man holding an umbrella, in a simple line drawing, without much detailing. He illustrates the male figure in quick and sharp strokes, defining the contours of his form.

metadata.inscription: There is a mark of the personal seal of the artist in black colour in the bottom-left corner of the sketch.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 8
artworks.description: In this delicate pencil sketch, Nandalal records a cart, an oft-seen element of rural life, often attached to a pair of bullocks. The fine blending of strokes lends it a soft, ephemeral quality.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: In this postcard Nandalal portrays a quick line drawing of three human figures sitting on the ground, probably asking for alms. The sharp and crisp pencil strokes define the contours of the forms. Nandalal carefully brings out the underlying emotion of dismay on the face of the man in front.

metadata.inscription: There is a mark of the personal seal of the artist in black colour in the bottom-left corner of the sketch.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: This postcard sketch shows a mother and child, rendered in delicate sweeping lines, without much detailing. To portray the tender moment, Nandalal delineates the fluid strokes in a calligraphic manner, a technique he acquired from the arts of the Far East.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and numbered '5' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: The postcard portrays a woman sitting beneath an umbrella, sketched in thick fluid lines defining the contours of the forms. The smudged shading over the body probably suggests the dark complexion of the figure.

metadata.inscription: There is a mark of the personal seal of the artist in black colour in the bottom-right corner of the sketch.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: In this postcard, Nandalal portrays a man and an infant walking in shallow waters, rendered in blunt strokes, defining the contours of the forms. The use of smudged lines adds rhythm, vigour and life to the form of the figures.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali, dated '6.1.18' in English and numbered '4' in the top-right corner of the sketch.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: In this postcard, Nandalal portrays a female figure, in delicate sweeping lines, defining the contours of her form. The swaying garments rendered in a calligraphic manner suggest a windy day at Kaligram, a small village in the Malda district of West Bengal.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '5.1.28' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is another inscription in English that reads, 'Kaligram', referring to the place it was sketched at.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: Nandalal had a strong affinity for sketching and drawing, instantly recording on post card sized papers the surrounding environs, people in their everyday life, flora and fauna or anything that he found fascinating. This postcard shows an anatomical line drawing of a human figure, drawn in thick and fluid contouring lines, without much detailing.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and numbered '8' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: In this postcard, Nandalal portrays a woman holding an earthen pot by her waist at a river bank, drawn in delicate sweeping lines, defining the contours of the form. The blunt calligraphic strokes accentuate the folds of the woman's saree.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '6.1.28' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is another inscription in Bengali that reads, "On the banks of the Nagor river" along the right margin.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: Nandalal preferred drawing from life, often sketching outdoors with the subject being life, nature studies, landscapes, figure drawings, animals or anything that he found fascinating.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and numbered '10' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: In this postcard, Nandalal renders a Buddhist monk from the north-eastern parts of India in an impressionistic manner, with uninterrupted flowing lines. The few confident strokes bring out the mature age and calm expression of the face.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and numbered '7' in the top-left corner of the sketch.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: In this postcard, Nandalal portrays the figure of a man with an outstretched arm, rendered in thick and smooth lines, defining the contours of the form. The dark sweeping strokes and their strong delineation in the calligraphic style accentuates the robust form of the figure.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and numbered '11' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: In this postcard, Nandalal portrays a boatman with an oar, drawn in thick and dark contouring lines. The quick and strong strokes rendered in the form accentuate the vigour and strength of the man as he rows.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and numbered '13' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: Nandalal's small sketches vastly vary in detailing, some drawn quickly with just a few lines, others executed with more elaborate characteristics from an analytical perspective. In this postcard, he has rendered an anatomical line drawing of a man leaning on one leg, probably over a wall, rendered in thick and fluid contouring lines.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali in the bottom-right corner of the sketch.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: This postcard shows a profile sketch of a man's face rendered in thick contouring lines. The blunt and coarse, rhythmic pencil strokes add vigour and life to the robust form of the face.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bnegali and numbered '18' in the bottom-left corner of the sketch.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: Nandalal Bose was indefatigable in his sketching routines which formed an adjunct part of his daily life. This postcard sketch shows an anatomical line drawing of a man in a certain action, drawn in fluid contouring lines. The brief moment has been captured in a few confident pencil strokes by the artist.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and numbered '15' in the bottom-left corner of the sketch.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: Nandalal explored a wide range of traditions to arrive at his unique visual language and has left behind a large corpus of works in a wide variety of styles, expressions and techniques. In this postcard, he has rendered a quick sketch of a figure in thick and broken contouring lines.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '8.11.17' in English in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is another inscription in English that reads, "From M. Dey's (Mukul Dey) sketch".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: In this postcard, Nandalal renders a profile sketch of a man’s face in an impressionistic manner, with quick, scribbled strokes. The fluid handling of the line and its strong delineation in a calligraphic style was the influence of the Far Eastern art practices in the artist’s works.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and numbered '19' in the bottom-left corner of the sketch.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: This postcard sketch shows two female figures, rendered in delicate sweeping lines. It is a quick sketch of a few confident lines, without much detailing. Nandalal, with subtle handling and soft delineation of the line, carefully studies the rhythmic and lean pattern in the shape and contours of the forms.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '8.11.17' in English in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is another inscription in English that reads, 'From M. Dey's (Mukul Dey) Sketch'.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: In this postcard sketch, Nandalal has depicted portraits of three men, giving different facial expressions. The fluid handling of the line and the smudged ink strokes suggest the contours of the faces, highlighting the facial features and demeanour of the subject.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali along the left margin of the sketch. The sketch bears three inscription in Hindi that reads as, 'Hawa, Samhoj, Nanhu' (referring to the name of the person) along the right margin of the sketch.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: Nandalals small sketches vastly vary in detailing, some drawn quickly with just a few lines, others executed with more elaborate characteristics from an analytical perspective. This postcard sketch shows an anatomical line drawing of an adolescent boy, tracing his movement, drawn in thick contouring lines. The brief moment has been captured in a few confident pencil strokes by the artist.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and numbered '16' on the top-left corner of the sketch.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: This postcard sketch by Nandalal shows an aged, turbaned man bent over in a pensive mood. The image portrays a moment captured in a few confident strokes.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and numbered '22' along the lower margin of the sketch.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: Nandalal's small sketches vastly vary in detailing, some drawn quickly with just a few lines, others executed with more elaborate characteristics from an analytical perspective. In this postcard, he renders a sage in detailed wiry lines, defining the contours of his body. His mature age is conveyed through the rugged and coarse strokes.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and numbered '24' in the bottom-left corner of the sketch.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: In this postcard, Nandalal sketches the station master of Nalhati, a town in the Birbhum district of West Bengal, rendered in fine contouring lines. Jaya Appasamy in her article, 'Nandalal Bose- Master Draughtsman' writes, "The drawings on postcards have a spontaneity and brevity not seen in more formal works. They exist as evidence of the artist's unceasing desire to master visual data."

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali along the left margin of the sketch. There is another inscription in English that reads, 'Station Master, Nalhaty, June 1920'.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: In this postcard, Nandalal renders a profile sketch of a man's face in a few delicate and confident lines, defining the contours of the form. The fluid handling of the line and its strong delineation in the calligraphic style was the influence of the Far Eastern art practices in the artist's work.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and numbered '25' in the bottom-left corner of the sketch.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: In this postcard, Nandalal sketches a man engrossed in making glass objects, rendered in the Far-Eastern style of ink paintings. The translucent quality of the ink lends a softness to the thick contouring outlines and swift and free brushwork, defining the contours of the forms.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' and numbered '27' in the bottom-left corner of the sketch.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: This postcard sketch by Nandalal shows men sleeping while crouched on train berths, rendered in loose outlines. It is a quick sketch executed with a few confident strokes defining the contours of the forms. Rough shading has been used to suggest chiaroscuro.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '28.10.17' along the lower margin of the sketch. There is another inscription in Bengali that can be translated as, "in the train".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: In this postcard, Nandalal sketches an idol maker crafting idols of Buddha at Ghum, a small hill town in the Darjeeling district of West Bengal, India, where Tibetan Buddhism is followed. Nandalal renders the sketch in delicate and flowing outlines of ink, defining the contours of the forms.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and numbered '28' in the bottom-left corner of the sketch. There is another inscription in Bengali that reads, 'Ghum' referring to the place it was sketched at.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: This postcard sketch shows a woman carrying a basket on her back, rendered in thick and dark smudging of the pencil. Dinkar Kowshik in his essay 'Drawings and Sketches of Nandalal' in the book, 'Nandalal Bose- A collection of Essays' writes, "Much of his (Nandalal's) strength and sensitive wealth finds expression in the spontaneity of his sketches. They are a veritable treasure of shrewd observation, powerful calligraphy, psychological insight, rich sallies of humour and emphatic portrayal of the flora and fauna."

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and numbered '29' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: Nandalal Bose was indefatigable in his sketching routines that formed an adjunct part of his daily life. In this postcard, the artist renders an anatomical line drawing of an adolescent in action, drawn with a few quick and confident strokes.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and numbered '30' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: In this postcard, Nandalal sketches a musician from Kursiung (now Kurseong), a hill-station near Darjeeling. Rendered with short, sharp strokes that define the contours of the form, the face has been softened with calligraphic lines accentuating the calm, ecstatic expression.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali, twice, in both corners along the bottom of the sketch. There is another inscription in English that reads, "Kursiung" (now Kurseong, a hill-station located in the Darjeeling district of West Bengal, India), referring to the place it was sketched at.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: In this postcard sketch, Nandalal has portrayed a woman, grinding raw turmeric on a stone slab as the inscription suggests. Rendered with delicate sweeping outlines that define the contours of her form, the quick calligraphic strokes add vigour and life.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and numbered '31' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is another inscription in Bengali that can be translated as, "raw turmeric".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: Nandalal is known to have fervently sketched on postcard sized papers recording his surroundings throughout his life. In this image, he has rendered from the back, a man sitting on a couch as he reads a book. Drawn with a few soft delineating lines that define the contours of the form, it conveys the ease and calm of the moment.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and numbered '32' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: Nandalal's small sketches vastly vary in detailing, some drawn quickly with just a few lines, others executed with more elaborate characteristics from an analytical perspective. In this postcard, he sketches a line drawing of a woman squatting on the ground, portrayed with loose strokes from the back.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and numbered '37' in the bottom-left corner of the sketch. There is another inscription in English that reads, "Kargpur" (now Kharagpur, an important industrial town in the Midnapore district of West Bengal, India) and is dated '6.7.23'.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: This postcard sketch by Nandalal shows an anatomical line drawing of a woman sitting in a certain posture, rendered with loose pencil strokes, defining only the outlines. Jaya Appasamy in her article, 'Nandalal Bose- Master Draughtsman' in the book, '?Nandalal Bose (1882-1966) Centenary Exhibition?' writes, "The drawings on postcards have a spontaneity and brevity not seen in more formal works. They exist as evidence of the artist's unceasing desire to master visual data."

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali in the bottom-left corner of the sketch. There is another inscription in English, that reads, "Kargpur" (now Kharagpur, an important industrial town in the Midnapore district of West Bengal, India) and dated '4.2.23' in English.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: In this postcard, Nandalal has sketched a quick anatomical line drawing of a figure squatting on the ground, holding a staff, rendered in rough, thick strokes. Drawings such as these served as studies of postures for the artist.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali, twice, in both corners along the bottom of the sketch. There is another inscription in English that reads, "Kargpur" (now Kharagpur, an important industrial town in the Midnapore district of West Bengal, India) and the sketch has been dated '6.7.23'.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: In this postcard, Nandalal sketches a quick anatomical line drawing of a man sitting, rendered in soft and loose outlines. Drawings such as these were meant to serve as studies of postures for the artist.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bnegali and dated '6/7/23' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is another inscription in English that reads, "Kargpur" (now Kharagpur, an important industrial town in the Midnapore district of West Bengal, India), referring to the place it was sketched at.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: This postcard shows an anatomical line drawing of a man kneeling on the ground with his hands close to his chest, rendered in thick outlines. Drawings such as these served as studies of postures for the artist.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'N.L.Bose' and dated '4.7.1923' in English, in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is another inscription in English that reads, "Kargpur" (now Kharagpur, an important industrial town in the Midnapore district of West Bengal, India), referring to the place it was sketched at.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: In this postcard, Nandalal sketches a man carrying firewood slung over his shoulders, rendered in sharp, short strokes. The firm handling of the line add vigour and life to the man's body.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'N.L.Bose' and dated '5.7.23' in English in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is another inscription in English that reads, "Kargpur" (now Kharagpur, an important industrial town in the Midnapore district of West Bengal, India) referring to the place it was sketched at.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: In this postcard, Nandalal sketches an anatomical line drawing of woman squatting on the ground, with a stick in hand, rendered with quick, loose outlines.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'N.L.Bose' and dated '8.7.23' in English in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is another inscription in English that reads, "Khargpur" (now Kharagpur, an important industrial town in the Midnapore district of West Bengal, India) referring to the place it was sketched at.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: Nandalal's exploration of the different ways of delineating a line allowed him to experiment with its varying forms adding rhythm, vigour and life to the form of his figures. In this postcard, Nandalal portrays a female figure, in quick sweeping lines, defining the contours of her form.

metadata.inscription: Dated '13.2.21' in English and signed 'Nanda' in Bengali in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. The sketch bears two inscription in English that reads as, 'Gangta' (referring to the name of the place) and 'After day'.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: In this postcard, Nandalal sketches a woman accompanied by an infant, reading amidst a cluster of trees at Santiniketan. Rendered in fluid outlines defining the contours of the forms, the calm and peace in the environment resonates in the body of the woman.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali twice and dated twice, '4.11.1917' and '1940', in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is another inscription in Bengali that can be translated as, "First visit to Santiniketan".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: This postcard shows the sketch of a woman at work, drawn in delicate sweeping lines defining the slender contours of her body and the facial features. It is ambiguous whether this is a work of Asit Kumar Haldar as inscribed on the postcard.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'N.L.Bose' and dated '13.1.21' in English in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is another inscription in English, that reads, "From Asit H.(Asit Kumar Haldar)".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: In this postcard, Nandalal sketches a local woman of Dhaboli (Andhra Pradesh) or Bagh caves (Madhya Pradesh), as per the inscriptions, rendered in delicate sweeping lines, defining the contours of her slender body. The swift, calligraphic strokes accentuate the folds of the draped garment adding rhythm and vigour to her form.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '13.1.21' along the right margin of the sketch. There are two other inscriptions in Bengali, that read, "Dhaboli" and "Bagh".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: Nandalal Bose was indefatigable in his sketching routines that formed an adjunct part of his daily life. In this sketch. He portrays a man dressed up in a traditional costume. The fluid handling of the line and the soft pencil strokes suggest the modelling of the body and the facial features.

metadata.inscription: Dated '13.2.21' in English and signed 'Nanda' in Bengali in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. The sketch bears an inscription in Bengali that can be translated as, 'Pashand' (referring to the name of the person).

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No. 9
artworks.description: Nandalal's small sketches vastly vary in detailing, some drawn quickly with just a few lines, others executed with more elaborate characteristics from an analytical perspective. In this postcard, he sketches an adolescent playing the violin, rendered in simple and fluid contouring lines, without much detailing.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '1923' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch.

artworks.description: Nandalal has here depicted a dog as it pounces on a rabbit. The scene has been rendered in the style of ancient Egyptian art. Dogs in this kind of art, especially collared hunting dogs, such as this, were often portrayed along with kings, to convey their might, power and virility.

artworks.title: Animal Drawings - Copy from Egyptian Paitings

artworks.title: Animal Drawings - Copy from Egyptian Paitings
artworks.description: In this sketch, Nandalal has rendered a deer as it would be depicted in ancient Egyptian art. Although figures, both animal and human, were portrayed in more geometric, static forms in this style, this is a dynamic, lyrical rendering capturing a moment while the deer is in stride.

artworks.title: Animal Drawings - Copy from Egyptian Paitings
artworks.description: The collection of Nandalal includes a sketch of an ancient Egyptian art piece featuring a jackal. The most important god of this ancient civilization was Ra, who is often depicted pictorially as a jackal and frequently found painted on frescoes in tombs.

artworks.title: Animal Drawings - Copy from Egyptian Paitings

artworks.title: Animal Drawings - Copy from Egyptian Paitings
artworks.description: In this sketch, Nandalal has drawn a wolf in the style of ancient Egyptian art. Animals in this kind of art were depicted not only for decorative purposes, but also for their associations with gods. The wolf is often associated with the god of war, Wepwawet.

artworks.description: In this postcard, Nandalal sketches several renditions of a decorative swan, in swift and rhythmic outlines, defining the contours of the forms. As the inscription suggests, the images have been reproduced from the book, 'Illustrations of Metal Work in Brass & Copper, Mostly South Indian' by Edgar Thurston and Velayuda Asari and W.S. Hadaway.

metadata.inscription: There is an inscription in English that reads, "Illustration of metal work in Brass and Copper (South Indian), 732.09/T 42", in the top-left corner of the sketch and, "Figure 118, page 313, page 317", along the bottom margin.

artworks.title: A Sketch from Sketch Book No. 19
artworks.description: In this postcard, Nandalal sketches a swan, incorporated within a leaf pattern, with fine, delicate lines. Eminent artist A. Ramachandran in the book, 'Rhythms of India - The Art of Nandalal Bose' has made the following observation about Nandalal's drawings and sketches, "He made quick graphic impressions, often simplifying them to just a few lines as he sought to understand the inherent structure of what he was seeing. At times he recorded objects in a more analytical way, while at others he transformed them into visual codes of pattern."

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: In this sketch, Nandalal renders an anatomical line drawing of Pulakesi, a monarch of the Chalukya dynasty in the 6th century A.D. He has also rendered another sketch of a chauri-bearer alongside. As the inscriptions suggest, the images have been reproduced from part of a mural from the Ajanta caves.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '27.7.45' along the lower margin of the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, "Aj (Ajanta) and "Palakesi".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: In this card, Nandalal sketches an anatomical line drawing of Pulakesi, a monarch of the Chalukya dynasty in the 6th century A.D. It is a quick rendition of the king in a relaxed pose. As the inscription suggests, the image has been reproduced from part of a mural in cave no. 1 of the Ajanta caves.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '27.7.45', in the bottom-left corner of the sketch. There is also an inscription in English that reads, "Cave I, Aj (Ajanta), Palakesi".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: This image, being one of many posture studies done by Nandalal, depicts the stance of a female figure, probably a queen as implied by her attire. She holds a baby in her right arm while the rest of her frame is in profile suggesting she is engaged in a conversation. The sketch rendered in firm, successive strokes is reproduced from part of a mural from cave no. 17 of the Ajanta caves.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '27.7.45' below the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, "Aj(Ajanta), Cav XVII (cave no.17)", above the date.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here sketched a richly attired male figure, probably a prince rendered in strong, linear strokes, part of the panel that depicts the Bodhisattva Avalokiteswara, from cave no. 1 of the Ajanta caves. The mural depicts this royal figure making an offering of lilies to the Bodhisattva.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '27.7.45' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is also an inscription in English that reads, "Cave I".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal here sketches a man, probably a prince, sitting cross-legged on the floor, teaching or advising someone, as the stance suggests. It is a quick and rough rendition, reproduced from part of a mural from cave no. 9 of the Ajanta caves.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '27.7.45' below the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, "Cave IX, Aj (Ajanta)".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here rendered an anatomical line drawing of a male figure, probably a prince, with his hands folded, sitting on the floor. The image has been reproduced in quick rough strokes from part of a mural, from cave no. 9 of the Ajanta caves.

metadata.inscription: Dated '27.7.45' in English below the sketch. There is also an inscription in English that reads, "Aj (Ajanta), IX)".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here studied, in quick, bold strokes, the posture of a male musician, part of a mural from cave no. 17 of the Ajanta caves. The mural depicts the deity Indra gliding down through the clouds with his retinue, which includes musicians, to worship the Buddha.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '27.7.45' below the sketch. There is also an inscription in English that reads, "Aj (Ajanta), Cave XVII".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: In this anatomical line drawing, Nandalal studies and contrasts the seated postures of a man and a woman, with their hands folded. Rendered in brisk and coarse strokes, the drawings have been sketched from part of a mural from cave no. 9 of the Ajanta caves.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '27.7.45' along the left margin of the sketch. There are inscriptions in English that both read, "Aj (Ajanta), Cave IX".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here sketched an anatomical line drawing of a female figure, rendered in quick and blunt, fluid lines, probably part of the mural that depicts the Sankhapala Jataka, from cave no. 1 of the Ajanta caves. This particular scene depicts a lady listening in rapt attention to the sermon delivered by a king of Magadha, who turned an ascetic.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '27.7.45' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, "Ajanta, Cave I".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: In this anatomical line drawing, Nandalal has studied the posture of Pulakesi, a monarch of the Chalukya dynasty in the 6th century A.D., rendered in quick fluid lines. As the inscription suggests, the image has been reproduced from part of a mural from the Ajanta caves.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali below the sketch. There is also an inscription in English that reads, "Aj (Ajanta), Pulakesi".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here studied the posture of a female figure, rendered in bold and blunt strokes, reproduced from part of the Mahajanaka Jataka , from cave no.1 of the Ajanta caves. This particular part of the mural depicts Sivali (Mahajanaka's wife) and her retinue listening to Mahajanaka in bewilderment.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '27.7.45' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, "Ajanta, cave I".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here studied the posture of a figure in prostration, rendered in thick contouring lines, in an anatomical line drawing. As the inscription suggests, the image has been reproduced from part of a mural in cave no. 2 of the Ajanta caves.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '27.7.45' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, "Ajanta, Cave II".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here sketched an anatomical line drawing of two female figures in profile, quickly rendered in blunt yet fluid strokes. The artist has studied the grace and rhythm in the way the elongated bodies have been delineated. As the inscription suggests, the image has been reproduced from cave no. 17 of the Ajanta caves.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali, along the left margin of the sketch. There is also an inscription in English that reads, "Ajanta, cave XVII".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here rendered an anatomical line drawing of a female figure, rendered in coarse and blunt strokes, part of the Champeyya Jataka from cave no.1 of the Ajanta caves. This particular part of the mural depicts the royal palace of Champeyya, the king of Champa river, as he delivers a sermon to the king of Varanasi, and the royal attendants listen.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '27.7.45' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, "Ajanta, cave I".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here executed a quick anatomical line drawing of a horse with its rider. Roughly rendered in dark contouring lines, the artist studies the symmetry of the human form. The drawing is reproduced from part of a mural depicting 'The Sinhala Avadana', painted on the interior walls of cave no. 17 of the Ajanta caves.

metadata.inscription: There is an inscription in English that reads, "cave XVII, Ajanta" and dated '27.7.45' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here rendered an anatomical line drawing of two celestial figures, a female and a male and likened their forms to that of a fish. As the inscription suggests, the drawing has been sketched from part of a mural from cave no. 17 of the Ajanta caves.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '27.7.45', in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, "Ajanta, cave XVII".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here sketched the figure of Pulakesi, a 7th century monarch of the Chalukya dynasty, rendered in bold and blunt strokes. The king's bent posture and the hand on his knee hint at distress, while his right hand is formed in 'Karna mudra' which in Buddhism is the gesture of warding off evil. There is no mention of any cave number from which this particular image has been reproduced, however, the artist has specified 'Ajanta' on the drawing paper.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '27.7.45' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, "Pulakesi, Aj (Ajanta)".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Here, Nandalal has sketched Pulakesi, a monarch of the Chalukya dynasty in the 6th century A.D., standing in the tribhanga (tri-bent) pose. The figure is rendered in brisk, short strokes. Along the left margin of the sketch the artist has further studied simple anatomical line drawings.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '27.7.45' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, "Pulakesi, Aj (Ajanta)", below the sketch.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Here, Nandalal has studied an anatomical line drawing of a woman in a trance as she soulfully plays the drum strung around her neck. The sketch is roughly rendered with quick, bold strokes reproduced from part of a mural from cave no. 1 of the Ajanta caves.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '27.7.45' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, "Aj (Ajanta), cave I".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here studied the posture of a woman blowing a conch shell. The sketch is spared all details and reduced to a basic outline drawing rendered with bold strokes. The fluidity in lines accentuate the slender contours of the figure. As the inscription suggests, the drawing has been reproduced from cave no. 2 of the Ajanta caves.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and inscribed "Aj (Ajanta), cave II", along the right margin of the sketch. Dated '27.7.45' in the bottom-right corner.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: The illustration is an anatomical line drawing of a female figure in an animated posture. Nandalal has rendered the sketch with brisk and bold strokes grasping the movement of the form. As the inscription suggests, this drawing has been reproduced from part of a mural from cave no. 1 of the Ajanta caves.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and inscribed "Cave I, Aj (Ajanta)" along the left margin of the sketch. Dated '27.7.45' in the bottom-right corner.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here studied a female figure standing in a tribhanga (tri-bent) pose holding a fan, roughly rendered in strong yet flowing strokes, accentuating the slender body. As per the inscription, the drawing has been sketched from cave no. 16 of the Ajanta caves.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '27.7.45' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, "Aj (Ajanta), C.(cave), XVI".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: In this anatomical drawing, Nandalal has studied the posture of a male warrior figure, as he holds a sword in one hand and a shield in the other. Rendered in rough, bold lines, the sketch is intended to analyse movement and mobility of the human body. As the inscription suggests, the image has been reproduced from part of a mural in cave no. 17 of the Ajanta caves.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '27.7.45' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is also an inscription in English that reads, "Cave XVII, Ajanta".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here studied the stance of a male figure, as he holds an arrow. Rendered in bold and rugged strokes that accentuate the strength of the body, the image has been reproduced from cave no. 17 of the Ajanta caves, as the inscription suggests.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '27.7.45' in the bottom-right corner. There is also an inscription in English that reads, "C.(cave) XVII, Aj (Ajanta)".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here studied the stance of a female figure, probably holding a rosary in the right hand while her left hand is in the gyana mudra . The drawing is rendered in deep and bold flowing strokes from cave 1 of the Ajanta caves.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '29.7.45', in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, "Aj (Ajanta), cave I", along the left side of the sketch.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here sketched a male attendant holding an earthen pot, rendered in quick flowing lines, part of the mural that depicts the Mahajanaka-Jataka , from cave no.1 of the Ajanta caves. The mural shows two attendants pouring holy water from decorated pitchers over prince Mahajanaka , during a ceremonial bath before his coronation.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '29.7.45', in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, "Aj (Ajanta), cave I".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Here Nandalal sketches a scene, probably part of the mural that depicts the Ummagga Jataka (the story of a tunnel) from cave no. 1 of the Ajanta caves. The young person looking at the heads may be Mahaushadha, with his wife Amara at his back, roughly rendered in brisk and fluid contouring lines.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda'' in Bengali and dated '29.7.45' in English, in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, "Aj (Ajanta), cave I".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here sketched a female attendant holding a plate, rendered in brisk, short strokes, part of the mural that depicts the Mahajanaka-Jataka , from cave no. 1 of the Ajanta caves. The mural shows two male attendants pouring holy water from decorated pitchers over prince Mahajanaka , during a ceremonial bath before his coronation, while three maids wait in attendance.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '29.7.45' in English, in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, "Cave I, Aj (Ajanta)".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here studied the stance of a female attendant, rendered in bold and flowing contouring lines, part of the mural that depicts the Mahajanaka Jataka from cave no. 1 of the Ajanta caves. The mural shows attendants serving the prince Mahajanaka at his royal toilet before a ceremonial bath.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '29.7.45' in English, in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, "Cave I, Aj (Ajanta)".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here studied the posture of a male figure asking for alms, rendered in blunt yet fluid lines, part of the mural that depicts the Mahajanaka Jataka from cave no. 1 of the Ajanta caves. The mural shows attendants serving the prince at his royal toilet before a ceremonial bath while mendicants wait outside the pavilion for the customary alms.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '29.7.45' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is also an inscription in English that reads, "Aj (Ajanta), cave I".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here studied the stance of an attendant leaning on a staff. The slightly bent posture is roughly rendered in repetitive, fluid lines, reproduced from part of the mural that depicts the 'Mahajanaka Jataka' from cave no. 1 of the Ajanta caves. This particular scene of the mural depicts the ritual of lustration being performed on Prince Mahajanaka, who is served by palace attendants in his royal toilet.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '29.7.45' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, "Cave I , Aj (Ajanta)", along the right margin.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here studied the figure of an attendant, holding a water pot over his shoulder. The stiff form is roughly rendered in linear strokes, sparing the sketch of much detail. The drawing is reproduced from part of the 'Mahajanaka Jataka' mural from cave no. 1 of the Ajanta caves. This particular scene depicts the ritual of lustration being performed on Prince Mahajanaka, who is served by palace attendants at his royal toilet.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali along the right margin of the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, "Aj(Ajanta), cave I", above the signature.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: In this image, Nandalal has studied the posture of a female figure as she looks upwards. The sketch has been reproduced from part of a mural in cave no.1 of the Ajanta caves.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '29.7.45', along the right margin of the sketch. There is also an inscription in English that reads,"Aj (Ajanta), cave I".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.medium: Pen ink and pencil on paper
artworks.description: Nandalal has here sketched a royal figure with folded hands, probably a king listening to an ascetic, etched in sharp contouring lines, from cave no. 1 of the Ajanta caves.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '29.7.45', in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is also an inscription in English that reads, "Aj (Ajanta), cave I".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here sketched one of his many posture studies reproduced from the murals of the Ajanta caves. In this image, a male figure kneels down as if to seek blessings. Rendered in dark, rapid strokes, as per the inscription, the drawing has been reproduced from cave no. 1.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '29.7.45', along the right margin of the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, "Cave I, Aj(Ajanta)", above the date.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here studied the posture of a seated male figure, probably a Buddha as he assumes the dharmachakra pravartana mudra, the gesture of preaching, usually interpreted as setting the wheel of law in motion. The sketch has been rendered in bold flowing lines, accentuating the slender body beneath the robe, from cave no. 1 of the Ajanta caves.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '29.7.45', in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is also an inscription in English that reads, "I cave, Aj (Ajanta)".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: In the image above, Nandalal has studied the posture of a woman seated on the floor. She is depicted with a musical instrument, roughly rendered in quick and bold contouring lines. The image is etched from cave no. 1 of the Ajanta caves.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '29.7.45', in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, "I cave, Aj (Ajanta)", below the sketch.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here studied the stance of a female figure, as she stands leaning against a pillar. The sketch is etched from cave no. 1 of the Ajanta caves and is rendered in brisk flowing lines, accentuating the graceful, slender body.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '29.7.45', in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is also an inscription in English that reads, "I cave, Aj (Ajanta)".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here studied the posture of a woman playing the flute, part of the story of the Mahajanaka Jatak from cave no.1 of the Ajanta caves, rendered in deep, fluid lines that accentuate her voluptuous body. This particular scene of the mural depicts a show of dance and music arranged by Sivali (Mahajanaka's wife), in an attempt to keep him tied to worldly life.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '29.7.45', along the right margin of the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, "Aj (Ajanta) cave I".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here studied the posture of a celestial nymph as she sits gracefully, gazing upwards. The artist renders the sketch in dark contouring lines, bringing out the delicacy of her feminine form. This image is reproduced from part of a panel portraying the Bodhisattva Padmapani from cave no.1 of the Ajanta caves. In this particular scene, a Gandharva couple (only the consort shown here) is depicted watching the Bodhisattva from a hill-abode.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '28.7.45', in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, "Aj (Ajanta), cave I", along the right margin.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: In the image above, Nandalal studies the stance of a dancer, part of the story of the Mahajanaka Jataka etched from cave no. 1 of the Ajanta caves. The sketch is rendered in smooth flowing lines, accentuating the graceful movement of the slender body. This particular scene of the mural depicts a show of dance and music arranged by Sivali (Mahajanaka's wife), in an attempt to keep him tied to worldly life.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '28.7.45' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is another inscription in English that reads, "Aj (Ajanta), cave I".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here sketched a male figure, standing by a pillar. With features such as the wavy hair and lotus-like eyes, the figure is probably the Bodhisattva Padmapani, gestured to hold a padma (lotus) flower in his right hand. The artist has rendered the form in deep, fluid lines, reproducing it from a mural from cave no. 1 of the Ajanta caves.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '28.7.45', in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, "Aj(Ajanta), cave 1", along the right margin.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here sketched a mother and a child, reproduced from a mural from cave no. 1 of the Ajanta caves. This image, one of many human studies done by the artist, is roughly rendered in brisk contouring lines, sparing the sketch of any much detail.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '28.7.45', in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, "Aj (Ajanta), cave I", along the right margin.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here studied the posture as well as the symmetry of the human form. This image depicts a female figure, looking upwards, her gesture suggesting awe as she puts her left hand on her chest. Reproduced from part of a mural from cave no. 1 of the Ajanta caves, the drawing is rendered in quick, bold strokes.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '28.7.45', in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, "Cave I, Aj (Ajanta)", along the right margin.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here studied the posture of a female figure, seated gracefully on the ground as she leans on her right hand. The artist renders the figure with great fluency, accentuating the contours of her robust form with dark, firm lines. As per the inscription, the drawing has been reproduced from cave no. 1 of the Ajanta caves.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '28.7.45', in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, "Aj (Ajanta), cave I", along the right margin.

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here studied a female figure rendered in delicate, flowing lines, accentuating her slender body. The image has been reproduced from part of the mural that depicts the Mahajanaka Jataka from cave no. 1 of the Ajanta caves. This particular scene shows prince Mahajanaka served by attendants at his royal toilet, before the coronation ceremony.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '28.7.45' in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, "Cave I, Aj (Ajanta)".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here studied the posture of a richly attired king sitting on the floor, rendered in quick bold strokes, subtly bringing out the nuances of the form. The image has been reproduced from part of a mural from cave no. 1 of the Ajanta caves.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali and dated '28.7.45', in the bottom-right corner of the sketch. There is an inscription in English that reads, Aj (Ajanta), cave I".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: Nandalal has here studied a female figure, rendered in dark and bold strokes of the pencil, bringing out the contours of the robust form. Part of the Mahajanaka Jataka sketched from cave no.1 of the Ajanta caves, this particular scene of the mural depicts prince Mahajanaka , seated under a heavily ornamented pavilion. Two attendants give him a ceremonial bath with holy water before the coronation, while three maids stand in attendance.

metadata.inscription: Signed 'Nanda' in Bengali along the right margin of the sketch and dated '28.7.45', in the bottom-right corner. There is an inscription in English that reads, "Aj (Ajanta), cave I".

artworks.title: Sketch from Sketch Book No.22 - Ajanta Sketches
artworks.description: This sketch is reproduced from part of a panel, 'The Conversion of Nanda' from cave no. 1 of the Ajanta caves, that depicts the story of Nanda, one of many past lives of Buddha. The female figure is the wife of Nanda, Janapada Kalyani. Nandalal has here rendered the figure in dark, blunt strokes defining the contours of her body.

artworks.title: Study of Oriental Art - Sketch Book No. 25

The artist has rendered a well defined form of the animal and traced ferocity in its expressions. The drawing has been delineated in fine calligraphic brush strokes which exhibit the contours of the animal's body.

artworks.title: Study of Oriental Art - Sketch Book No. 25

Below this drawing, the artist has also made tracings of two people engaged in writing, possibly courtiers. The illustration has been reproduced in steady, bold lines with ink and brush from Ananda Coomaraswamy's book, Indian Drawings .

artworks.title: Study of Oriental Art - Sketch Book No. 25

metadata.inscription: There is an inscription in English that reads, 'Page.6, Fig.4. Mughal Portrait, 17th Cent (Century), Indian Drawing book' in the bottom-right corner of the drawing.

artworks.title: Study of Oriental Art - Sketch Book No. 25

metadata.inscription: There is an inscription in English that reads, 'Fig.18. Indian Drawings. A.K. Coomaraswamy' in the bottom-right corner of the drawing.

artworks.title: Study of Oriental Art - Sketch Book No. 25
artworks.description: Nandalal has here traced two compositions, probably from part of a Mughal miniature or old manuscript that are embellished with illuminated borders of animal and bird illustrations. In the upper tracing, a group of leaping deer can be seen rendered in fine, linear pencil strokes while in the lower tracing, a hunting scene with animal and bird figures has been depicted amidst an exquisite floral pattern. The figures are imbued with feeling and the use of fine lines adds grace to the whole composition.

artworks.title: Study of Oriental Art - Sketch Book No. 25
artworks.description: Nandalal has here reproduced the figure of a tamed rhinoceros with a string of bells around its neck. The textured surface of the hide and its folds has been depicted in a playful manner, in small round circles and curvilinear lines by the artist.

artworks.title: Study of Oriental Art - Sketch Book No. 25
artworks.description: Nandalal has here rendered two drawings, a moving lion and a roaring bull. Both are rendered in sharp, strong strokes and ferocity can be seen in their expressions that have been delineated in a few lines as the artist sought to understand the basic forms of the animals.

artworks.title: Study of Oriental Art - Sketch Book No. 25

artworks.title: Study of Oriental Art - Sketch Book No. 25
artworks.description: Nandalal has here made the drawing of a blackbuck, as she stands with her fawns, suckling one while the other looks over. The composition has been executed in dark and thick brush strokes with confidence and the shading lends a three-dimensional effect.

artworks.title: Study of Oriental Art - Sketch Book No. 25
artworks.description: Nandalal has here created a design which comprises the silhouette of a deer filled with an ornamental floral design. Linear pencil strokes depict the fine contours of the deer and the floral design has been executed in calligraphic lines. Jaya Appasamy elucidates in her essay, 'Nandalal- Master Draughtsman' in the book 'Nandalal Bose (1882-1966) Centenary Exhibition', "His design though based on natural forms was not naturalistic; it followed nature only as a starting point and developed into shapes and patterns imbued with abstract elements such as rhythm, movement, motifs and delicate details. He planned his designs as he would a composition: with attention to structure, on a division of mass and space, symmetry or asymmetry."

artworks.title: Study of Oriental Art - Sketch Book No. 25
artworks.description: Nandalal has here artistically composed an illustration or an ornamental design in which four deer that have individual bodies and stand in varied postures, have a common head. Linear pencil strokes depict the fine contours of the design and reflect the confidence and maturity of the artist. Jaya Appasamy in her essay, 'Nandalal- Master Draughtsman' in the book, 'Nandalal Bose (1882- 1966) Centenary Exhibition' elucidates, "His design though based on natural forms was not naturalistic; it followed nature only as a starting point and developed into shapes and patterns imbued with abstract elements such as rhythm, movement, motifs and delicate details. He planned his designs as he would a composition: with attention to structure, on a division of mass and space, symmetry or asymmetry."

artworks.title: Study of Oriental Art - Sketch Book No. 25
artworks.description: Nandalal has here created an ornamental design that consists of the figure of a leaping deer, rendered in fine, linear pencil strokes and surrounded with decorative creepers that have been drawn in ornate, calligraphic strokes. The artist has also studied the head of the deer separately in a small template sketch. Jaya Appasamy in her essay, 'Nandalal- Master Draughtsman' in the book, 'Nandalal Bose (1882-1966) Centenary Exhibition' elucidates about his art, "His design though based on natural forms was not naturalistic; it followed nature only as a starting point and developed into shapes and pattern imbued with abstract elements such as rhythm, movement, motifs and delicate details. He planned his designs as he would a composition: with attention to structure, on a division of mass and space, symmetry or asymmetry."

artworks.title: Study of Oriental Art - Sketch Book No. 25
artworks.description: Nandalal has here artistically rendered an illustration or an ornamental design that consists of three lions, that have individual bodies in various stances but a common head. The linear, fluid strokes depict the fine contours of the design and reflect the maturity of the artist. He has also rendered a quick sketch of two tigers fighting as a template above the main composition. Nandalal has elucidated in his book 'On Art', "In any artistic composition it is the line that gives unity and character to each object in the composition, as well as to all the objects taken together....Postures depend chiefly on the bend and movement of the backbone. This can be observed and studied properly if one takes a side view."

artworks.title: Kanchanjangha
artworks.description: In this painting Nandalal has rendered a view of Kanchanjangha. He has painted in deep tints of black, the distinctive shape of the mountains and used grey patches to give an impression of the mountain surrounded with mist. This painting is one of the landscapes in the monochrome ink wash technique, which is associated with specific Chinese and Japanese landscape traditions. It also recalls a statement from his book, 'Vision and Creation' on landscape painting, ''Landscapes can be painted in the manner of seas, with wavy heaps of stone and earth.''

artworks.title: Self Portrait
artworks.description: Bold eyes stare out, just a few black strokes give the sense of a strong personality – swathes of energetic red, purple, yellow and blue fit together like a jigsaw puzzle. You are looking at a self portrait by Francis Newton Souza, painted in his distinctive, emotive style. Souza’s unique form combined impressionism and expressionism with the spirit of cubism and the sculptures of classical Indian tradition. His work covered a range of subjects from Catholic Christian iconography -- that stemmed from his Goan Catholic roots -- to nudes, still life and landscapes. Souza’s work passed through various phases from the early days in Mumbai to a period of struggle, success and turmoil in London to international recognition and a more stable life in New York. But in every phase Souza’s art was invariably bold and exploratory. It was often dark, brutal and aggressive, but also erotic, sensual and touched with an ironic humour. Souza was a founder member of the influential Progressive Artists Group that included SH Raza and MF Husain and heralded a truly modern approach in Indian art. He died in Mumbai in 2002 at the age of 78.

artworks.description: It is interesting to see from the hundreds of sketches and drawings in the NGMA collection, how Roy broke down the figure to the essential form that goes into its making and then synthesised it to suggest a structure. In this particular are shown three men bearing religious markings on their forehead of the Vaishnavite sect. The sketches are evidences that Jamini Roy made meticulous sketches and drawings in great detail before undertaking a painting and that he chose to narrate imagery drawn from the village life, be it the peasants, artisans, followers of religious cults, women, etc.

artworks.title: Sketch-III
artworks.description: From the end 1920s, Jamini Roy rejected the European oil medium and began to use the traditional pigments from vegetable and mineral sources. The imagery was often drawn from village life. Jamini Roy invested in the portrayal of peasants, artisans, followers of religious cults, village women and adivasis with immense dignity. He represented in his paintings what they held sacred with references from folk tales and narratives that permeated the rural consciousness. In this particular sketch the artist has portrayed three men wielding swords and shields in their hands.

artworks.title: Sketch-II
artworks.description: It is interesting to see from the hundreds of sketches and drawings in the NGMA collection, how Roy broke down the figure to the essential form that goes into its making and then synthesised it to suggest a structure. Jamini Roy made meticulous sketches and drawings in great detail before undertaking a painting.

artworks.title: Sketch-IV
artworks.description: This sketch is an evocative image of a rural community. Divided into two panels the lower one depicts a group of Vaishnavas who go around villages singing kirtans (devotional songs) on the life of Krishna, and seeking alms. There is a nuance of ecstasy in the depiction of figure holding the stringed instrument and the accompanying singers. Roy conveys a sense of an idyll where faith, music and dance combine to create an organic wholeness in life. The upper panel portrays four figures in profile and also holding a dance pose. It is also interesting to see how Roy broke down the figure to the essential form that goes into its making and then synthesised it to suggest a structure. Jamini Roy often drew his imagery from village life narrating the life of the peasants, artisans, and followers of religious cults, village women and adivasis with immense dignity and representations that were authentic using simplification of form inspired by the folk arts of the region that had evolved over the centuries.

artworks.title: Sketch-VI
artworks.description: The large number of sketches and drawings in the NGMA collection give evidence of the distinctive way in which Jamini Roy structured his figures. Each figure is created by assembling a set of body parts which are broken down into simple forms only to be reclaimed as a whole. This sketch of a seated woman draped in a sari with her head covered in the collection of NGMA strongly points that Jamini Roy chose to narrate imagery drawn from the village life, be it the peasants, artisans, followers of religious cults, women, etc. The artist must have felt a sense of elation at finding his way back home because one observes an expression of joyous exuberance as he had found a way to communicate with the people.

artworks.title: Sketch-V
artworks.description: The sketches and drawings of Jamini Roy point to the artist's diverse experimentation with form. The sketches are certainly prototypes for some of his paintings. The sketches are also evidences of the artist's efforts and attempts through his long career to arrive at his unique style of painting using simple, pure forms.

artworks.title: The Last Painting
artworks.description: In the 1940s, Roy painted one of his most powerful series of images revolving around the life of Jesus Christ. Although, he may have painted occasional images of Christ in the previous decade, he developed the visual idea more fully in the 1940s. What was most thought-provoking about these paintings was Roy's skill in adapting stories from an alien culture and yet giving them a familiar appearance, as if they were people from our own villages. The language of the Christ painting is remarkable for other reasons as well. Roy invests the grave, contemplative faces in their somewhat hieratic poses with iconicity.

artworks.title: Two Pigeons
artworks.description: Ramkinkar Baij was a reclusive modernist artist who always remained on the fringes of the art market. He took a great interest in human figures, body language and in the general human drama. Modern Western art and pre and post-classical Indian art were his main points of reference. Although primarily known for his expressionistic sculpture, he was also a gifted painter. The sense of rhythm that his sculpture was noted for is manifested brilliantly in his paintings and sketches. His works in the Kalighat tradition interconnected with Cubism to achieve an unusual personal idiom. Both his sculpture and his paintings are unprompted and bold.

artworks.title: Painting
artworks.description: Vasudeo S. Gaitonde,one of the pioneering figure in shaping Indian Modern art scene, was born in 1924 in Maharashtra. He studied art at Sir J.J. School of Art, Mumbai and obtained a diploma in 1948. He impressed the likes of the progressive artists of the time like F.N Souza, S.H Raza and M.F Husain, and was invited to join the Progressive Artist Group in 1950. Today Gaitonde is recognised for his non-representational art; but he started off by painting stylised figures and gradually made his transition to the abstract art attaining the ethereal lyricism and poetry. He used limited colours and mostly the hues and gradation of the same colour to depict his subjects which ultimately would become a fraction of the painting. Gaitonde was inspired from post-war artists like Paul Klee, Wassily Kandinsky, and Joan Miro. His works are in the collection of National Gallery of Modern Art, New Delhi, Lalit Kala Akademi, New Delhi, Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, Mumbai, Museum of Modern Art, New York, Pundole Art Gallery, Mumbai, Mr. Bal Chhabda, Mumbai.

Musical Construction, 1967
artworks.description: Dhanraj Bhagat played with different genres, techniques and mediums like wax, plaster of paris, wood, papier mache, aluminium, copper, cement with iron filings and even a combination of wood and steel as in a 1967 sculpture titled 'Musical Construction', keeping his art well beyond the quagmire of definitions. Dhanraj Bhagat presents his audience with a unique perspective of seeing the human body. This understanding represented in his sculptural work prizes structure over realism even as he works at deconstructing the values of art conventions to create his own language in the ways of seeing and sculpting. In many sculptures on view, we are left to discover the relationship between modern and contemporary art styles to form a creative and conceptual niche that exalted the beauty and poise of the human figure both as a realist entity as well as an abstract study that sought to define new dimensions. Bhagat’s rhythmic, abstract and sensitively sculpted figures preserve traditional subject matter of the human body as well as heightens its potential to explore new boundaries and express eternal evocations. Critic Richard Bartholomew recorded that Bhagat abandoned the sensuous for the spiritual as he traversed a progressive path of evolution.
